title: Senior/Staff Machine Learning Research Scientist, Generative Modeling for Planning — Nuro — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
text:
Senior/Staff Machine Learning Research Scientist, Generative Modeling for Planning — Nuro — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
User Research
Senior/Staff Machine Learning Research Scientist, Generative Modeling for Planning
Lead generative-modeling research for planning in Nuro's autonomous driving platform.
What the role actually is
Nuro is hiring a senior or staff research scientist for generative modeling in planning. The role targets the research layer behind autonomy decisions: modeling possible futures, improving planning quality, and validating learned methods for real vehicles.
The seniority suggests this person would influence research direction as well as implementation. It is a fit for researchers who want their work to shape deployed physical AI systems.
What you would work on
Set research direction for generative modeling approaches to planning
Build and evaluate learned planners for autonomous driving use cases
Connect model behavior to safety, simulation, and production-readiness constraints
Collaborate across autonomy, infrastructure, and evaluation teams
What they are asking for
Senior research experience in ML, autonomy, robotics, or planning
Depth in generative modeling or learning-based decision-making
Ability to lead ambiguous research work toward practical outcomes
Strong judgment about evaluating models in safety-critical physical systems
Why this one is worth a look
This is the more senior version of a theme showing up across autonomy teams: learned planning is becoming central, but the hard part is proving that it behaves well enough outside the benchmark.

Boston Dynamics is hiring a senior staff product marketing manager for Atlas in Waltham. The role owns announcements, go-to-market plans, product positioning, launch content, sales collateral, and customer-facing storytelling for the humanoid program.

title: Senior/Staff Systems Engineer, Autonomy Verification — Nuro — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
text:
Senior/Staff Systems Engineer, Autonomy Verification — Nuro — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
User Research
Senior/Staff Systems Engineer, Autonomy Verification
Define requirements, metrics, and test strategy to prove Nuro's autonomous driver is safe for its target ODD.
What the role actually is
Nuro is hiring a senior or staff systems engineer for autonomy verification. The role owns requirements, metrics, acceptance criteria, and test strategy for proving the Nuro Driver can operate safely in its target operating design domain and follow rules of the road.
This belongs on the board because it is evaluation work for robot behavior: deciding what evidence is required before autonomy can ship.
What you would work on
Create requirements for safe autonomous operation within Nuro's target ODD
Design metrics and acceptance criteria for autonomy behavior and rules-of-road compliance
Use simulation, logs, closed-course tests, and accident reconstructions to verify requirements
Collaborate with behavior, perception, data science, product, legal, and public trust teams
Own the verification strategy from requirements definition through evidence generation
What they are asking for
Experience developing or validating autonomous systems
Ability to define requirements, metrics, and acceptance criteria for complex behavior
Familiarity with safety standards, testing methodologies, simulation, or autonomy evaluation
Strong cross-functional collaboration with autonomy software, simulation, product, and operations teams
Systems-level judgment about what makes robot behavior deployable
Why this one is worth a look
Autonomy evaluation is where product claims meet proof. Nuro's role is notable because it treats behavior metrics and verification strategy as first-class work, not an afterthought once the autonomy stack is built.

Senior Staff Technical Program Manager
Drive release and test programs for Hivemind Enterprise, Shield AI's autonomy SDK for unmanned systems.
What the role actually is
Shield AI is hiring a senior staff TPM for Hivemind Enterprise, the software development kit used to build unmanned systems and mission applications. The role centers on software quality, simulation-based test automation, release management, and flight-test operations.
This is a product execution role for autonomy software: the person would coordinate product managers, designers, customer-facing teams, and engineering groups so complex releases ship with enough evidence behind them.
What you would work on
Drive planning and delivery for Hivemind Enterprise software releases
Build rigorous simulation-based test automation programs for autonomy software
Coordinate test operations from CI through hardware-in-the-loop and flight test
Define scope, milestones, risks, owners, and release-readiness criteria
Work with product, design, customer engagement, and engineering teams on delivery quality
What they are asking for
Senior TPM, engineering management, or software test leadership experience
Background with complex software, integrated hardware/software systems, AI, or robotics
Ability to run release management and test operations across multiple technical teams
Strong communication and ownership in high-stakes autonomy programs
Why this one is worth a look
Hivemind Enterprise is Shield AI's attempt to make autonomy software usable beyond one internal aircraft program. The role is worth watching because simulation, test automation, and release discipline are what decide whether an autonomy platform can actually be adopted by other teams.

Bias toward turning test results into actionable deployment evidence

title: Sr. Technical Program Manager, Hardware/Software Integration — Serve Robotics — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
text:
Sr. Technical Program Manager, Hardware/Software Integration — Serve Robotics — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
Product
Sr. Technical Program Manager, Hardware/Software Integration
Coordinate Serve's robot hardware, software, manufacturing test, and deployment programs for fleet upgrades and new features.
What the role actually is
Serve Robotics is hiring a senior TPM for hardware and software integration. The role coordinates technical projects that move across mechanical, electrical, embedded, systems, manufacturing, software, and operations teams.
The product surface is the deployed sidewalk delivery robot. This person would help plan robot upgrades, product-development processes, manufacturing test work, and new feature delivery across a distributed organization.
What you would work on
Plan and track hardware/software integration programs for Serve's delivery robots
Coordinate mechanical, electrical, embedded, systems, manufacturing, software, and operations teams
Improve hand-offs for components, robots, software, testing, and deployment
Identify roadblocks and process gaps in fleet upgrades and feature development
What they are asking for
Senior TPM experience with hardware/software products or robotics systems
Ability to understand technical systems deeply enough to spot integration risk
Strong cross-functional communication across engineering, manufacturing, and operations
Experience building repeatable processes for complex technical delivery
Why this one is worth a look
Serve is operating real sidewalk robots in multiple U.S. cities, so integration work has a direct path to the fleet. This is less about speculative robotics and more about making deployed robots improve without breaking the operating machine around them.

Serve Robotics
Sidewalk delivery robotics company deploying autonomous robots for last-mile delivery in U.S. cities.

title: Senior Technical Program Manager — Agility — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
text:
Senior Technical Program Manager — Agility — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
Product
Senior Technical Program Manager
Lead operations programs that connect Agility's humanoid engineering work to scalable production.
What the role actually is
Agility Robotics is hiring a senior technical program manager in its operations program management group. The role leads programs across engineering, supply chain, procurement, manufacturing, quality, and external partners as Agility scales production.
This is a product-adjacent operations program role for humanoid robotics. It is about making the engineering intent behind Digit's platform survive the operational reality of suppliers, factories, quality systems, and production cadence.
What you would work on
Lead complex programs at the intersection of engineering, operations, and supply chain
Build mechanisms that help Agility move from early-stage work to running production
Coordinate supplier, procurement, manufacturing, quality, hardware, and product dependencies
Track program risks and decisions that affect robot production scale
Turn ambiguous operational needs into clear program plans and ownership
What they are asking for
Technical program management experience with hardware, robotics, manufacturing, or operations programs
Ability to work across supply chain, procurement, manufacturing engineering, quality, hardware, and product
Strong execution, risk management, and cross-functional leadership skills
Comfort with a hybrid role centered on Agility's Salem office
Why this one is worth a look
For humanoids, the hard part is not only whether the robot can do the task. It is whether the company can build and support enough reliable robots for the task to matter. This role is right in that scaling problem.
About
Agility
U.S. humanoid robotics company behind Digit and Arc, focused on deployed warehouse and manufacturing automation.

Product
Senior Technical Program Manager, Robot Skills Development
Lead execution for Agility's robot skills roadmap, balancing deployed customer needs with reusable humanoid capabilities.
What the role actually is
Agility is hiring a senior TPM embedded with the team that turns robot behaviors into reusable skills for Digit deployments. The role sits between product management, software, AI engineering, solutions engineering, and fleet orchestration.
This is product-adjacent program work rather than generic project tracking. The person would turn a robot skills roadmap into execution plans while balancing urgent deployment fixes against longer-term platform capabilities.
What you would work on
Translate the robot skills roadmap into milestones, scope, and delivery plans
Coordinate dependencies across robot software, AI engineering, solutions, and fleet orchestration teams
Balance near-term deployment needs with reusable manipulation, perception, and controls capabilities
Create operating structure for a team building adaptable robot behaviors
What they are asking for
Technical program management experience with complex software or robotics systems
Ability to work closely with product managers and senior engineering leaders
Comfort managing ambiguous dependencies across multiple technical teams
Judgment around tradeoffs between customer delivery and platform scaling
Why this one is worth a look
The interesting part is the productization problem: Agility has to turn individual humanoid behaviors into a library of skills that can survive real customer environments. A TPM in this seat helps decide how much of today's deployment pain becomes tomorrow's reusable robot capability.

Senior Technical Program Manager - Robotics — Pickle Robot — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
Product
Senior Technical Program Manager - Robotics
Drive software program execution for Pickle's autonomous warehouse robotics platform across robotics, firmware, hardware, and deployment.
What the role actually is
Pickle Robot is hiring a senior TPM inside its software engineering organization. The role coordinates software initiatives for autonomous warehouse robots, with close ties to robotics, firmware, hardware, product, manufacturing, and deployment teams.
This is a hands-on execution role for getting warehouse robot software shipped cleanly. The person would keep roadmaps, sprint plans, releases, risks, and cross-functional dependencies moving in the same direction.
What you would work on
Lead planning and delivery for software programs across Pickle's robotics platform
Coordinate robotics, firmware, hardware, product, manufacturing, and deployment work
Identify technical risks, dependencies, and tradeoffs before they block delivery
Improve release planning, roadmap reviews, sprint planning, and program reviews
What they are asking for
Senior technical program management experience with software-heavy technical products
Strong technical foundation, ideally from software engineering or close engineering partnership
Ability to bring structure to startup programs with changing priorities
Comfort working onsite with robotics, hardware, product, and deployment teams
Why this one is worth a look
Pickle's product lives in production warehouses, where software quality shows up as throughput and downtime rather than abstract metrics. This role is useful for someone who wants robotics program work close to real deployment pressure.

Product
Senior Technical Program Manager, Software
Coordinate software delivery for Proxie across autonomy, robot behaviors, and fleet management at Collaborative Robotics.
What the role actually is
Collaborative Robotics is hiring a senior TPM for the software behind Proxie. The scope includes autonomy, localization, perception, navigation, robot behaviors, and fleet management across current and future robot generations.

Plan and track software programs for Proxie's autonomy stack and fleet systems

Technical program management experience with complex software or robotics programs
Ability to work across autonomy, robot behavior, platform, and fleet-management teams
Strong planning, communication, and issue-resolution skills
Comfort operating onsite with cross-functional robot product teams
Why this one is worth a look
Collaborative Robotics is building around human-robot interaction rather than isolated automation cells. This seat is a practical way into that problem: making the software roadmap for a social, mobile robot coherent enough to ship.

title: Senior UX Researcher, Fauna — Fauna Robotics — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
text:
Senior UX Researcher, Fauna — Fauna Robotics — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
User Research
Senior UX Researcher, Fauna
Build the research practice for Fauna's everyday robots, from lab studies and field work to experience metrics.
What the role actually is
Fauna is hiring a senior UX researcher to define how it studies everyday interaction with physical robots. The role owns the research practice around a new product category: recruiting, protocols, lab and field studies, prototype evaluation, and metrics that tell the team whether the robot is becoming more understandable and welcome.
This is a rare robotics research role where the research object is not only task success. It is also comfort, trust, first-run experience, longitudinal use, and the messy reality of robots sharing ordinary human spaces.
What you would work on
Decide which product risks and interaction questions need research first
Run lab, field, concept, prototype, and longitudinal studies for embodied robot experiences
Define experience metrics across first use, task success, satisfaction, and retention signals
Turn research findings into decisions with design, product, and engineering
What they are asking for
Senior user research experience with full ownership of study design, recruiting, moderation, analysis, and reporting
Experience with field research, ethnography, lab testing, prototype testing, concept testing, and survey design
Quantitative and qualitative research fluency, including behavioral data and statistics
Familiarity with human-robot interaction, agentic systems, embodied products, or in-home research
Why this one is worth a look
Fauna is the Amazon-owned robotics team aiming at robots for everyday human environments rather than warehouse automation alone. That makes the research challenge unusually broad: the team has to learn what people will tolerate, trust, enjoy, and come back to when the product has a body in the room.

title: Senior Video Producer — Zipline — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
text:
Senior Video Producer — Zipline — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
Marketing
Senior Video Producer
Lead video storytelling that explains Zipline's autonomous delivery service as it expands in the U.S.
What the role actually is
Zipline is hiring a senior video producer on its communications and marketing side. The role is about making complex autonomous delivery work understandable through customer stories, launch narratives, service explainers, and public-facing video.
Video matters here because drone delivery is a physical experience. The person would help show how the system works, why communities should care, and what the service feels like when it reaches real customers.
What you would work on
Produce video stories for Zipline's communications, launches, and brand channels
Translate autonomous logistics, customer impact, and community adoption into visual narratives
Coordinate production plans, shoots, edits, reviews, and delivery across teams
Work with communications, marketing, creative, operations, and local launch teams
What they are asking for
Video production experience for brand, communications, documentary, launch, or customer storytelling
Strong editorial judgment and ability to simplify complex technical subjects
Comfort managing production logistics, stakeholders, schedules, and approvals
Interest in telling grounded stories about robotics, logistics, healthcare, retail, or public service
Why this one is worth a look
Robotics companies need proof people can see. For Zipline, video can make the difference between an abstract drone-delivery claim and a service people understand. This role sits directly in that storytelling layer.

User Research
Software Engineer V, Applied ML Research
Own applied ML research for robotic grasping in Pickle Robot's truck-unloading systems.
What the role actually is
Pickle Robot is hiring a senior applied ML researcher to own how its truck-unloading robot decides what to grasp and how to grasp it. The posting describes a small team working at the intersection of classical robotics and neural networks.
This is a staff-level software title, but the job is explicitly about applied ML research for physical robot manipulation.
What you would work on
Set direction for grasp selection and manipulation ML in warehouse robots
Fuse classical robotics methods with neural-network-based approaches
Work on real systems that unload trucks and containers alongside warehouse teams
Help expand autonomy toward broader logistics workflows over time
What they are asking for
Deep experience with ML systems and real robot platforms
Strong judgment about manipulation, grasping, or physical AI methods
Ability to choose approaches independently in a senior technical seat
Interest in practical robotics problems inside logistics environments
Why this one is worth a look
Truck unloading is unglamorous but brutally real robotics. Pickle's role is compelling because it gives one person unusually clear ownership of a hard manipulation problem with immediate operational consequences.

title: Sr Deployment Program Manager, Robotics — Collaborative Robotics — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
text:
Sr Deployment Program Manager, Robotics — Collaborative Robotics — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
Product
Sr Deployment Program Manager, Robotics
Lead customer deployments, onsite testing, and cross-functional launch plans for Collaborative Robotics' robot fleets.
What the role actually is
Collaborative Robotics is hiring a senior deployment program manager to own the path from project plan to working robot fleet at customer sites. The role is remote within the U.S. and expects regular travel for implementation, testing, and customer coordination.
This is program management close to the product surface: the person has to coordinate engineering, solutions, operations, sales, and customer teams while turning deployment lessons into repeatable processes.
What you would work on
Oversee onsite testing and readiness work for robot fleets before customer launch
Coordinate scope, milestones, schedules, risk mitigation, and delivery across internal and external teams
Work directly with customers to understand operational requirements and deployment constraints
Turn lessons from pilots and launches into improved workflows, documentation, and process changes
What they are asking for
Program or project management experience with end-to-end accountability for multiple technical projects
Experience deploying robotics, automation, or related systems in real customer environments
Working understanding of robotic systems, hardware/software integration, and deployment methods
Ability to communicate clearly with customers, engineers, operations teams, and leadership
Why this one is worth a look
Collaborative Robotics is explicitly designing robots around human environments. This role is interesting because it sits where the company's HRI promise has to survive the messy parts of real deployment: customer workflows, fleet prep, travel, troubleshooting, and repeatability.

Collaborative Robotics
Santa Clara robotics company building collaborative robots designed to work in human environments.

title: Sr Product Manager, Assisted Autonomy — Kodiak — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
text:
Sr Product Manager, Assisted Autonomy — Kodiak — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
Product
Sr Product Manager, Assisted Autonomy
Own Kodiak's assisted-autonomy product for human-in-the-loop control of autonomous trucks in defined scenarios.
What the role actually is
Kodiak is hiring a senior product manager for Assisted Autonomy, the part of its autonomous trucking system where a human can remotely control a truck in low-speed, clearly defined scenarios. The role owns the product direction for that human-in-the-loop layer.
This is an IC product role that blends software, hardware, field operations, customer feedback, safety, and UX/design judgment. The listing is explicit that the work includes highly usable interfaces for teleoperations and non-technical users.
What you would work on
Formulate and evolve the Assisted Autonomy roadmap across near-term deployment and long-term scale
Define requirements with engineering, operations, safety, program, and customer-facing teams
Improve software interfaces for dispatch, telestation capabilities, and related hardware integrations
Use operational data and KPIs to prioritize failure modes and safety improvements
Visit deployment locations to gather customer and field feedback
What they are asking for
Product management experience in software and hardware environments
Experience launching high-tech, end-user-facing products at scale
Strong UX/design judgment for teleoperation and human-in-the-loop workflows
Ability to reason clearly about data, KPIs, product tradeoffs, and field deployment
Prior exposure to assisted autonomy, autonomous vehicles, or robotics
Why this one is worth a look
Assisted autonomy is where the clean story of self-driving meets operational reality. This role is interesting because it treats human control as a product surface, not an exception path: what the remote operator sees, when they intervene, and how the system earns trust.

Kodiak
Mountain View autonomous trucking company building self-driving software for commercial freight and public-sector ground vehicles.

title: Staff Hardware Technical Program Manager — Agility — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
text:
Staff Hardware Technical Program Manager — Agility — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
Product
Staff Hardware Technical Program Manager
Lead cross-functional execution for Agility's next-generation humanoid hardware platforms from concept through launch.
What the role actually is
This Staff TPM owns the operating cadence for Agility's next-generation humanoid hardware programs. The work sits between product definition, hardware engineering, operations, go-to-market, service, and launch readiness.
What you would work on
Build the integrated program plan across concept, architecture, prototype builds, validation, production, and general availability
Track critical path milestones, dependencies, build readiness, and release commitments across hardware, firmware, operations, and service
Surface long-lead component risks, resourcing gaps, and technical trade-offs early enough for teams to act
Create execution frameworks that make complex robot hardware delivery more predictable
What they are asking for
Staff-level technical program management experience on complex hardware products
Comfort coordinating multidisciplinary engineering, operations, service, and commercial teams
Experience with hardware development phases such as EVT, DVT, PVT, production readiness, or launch execution
Ability to translate technical risk and schedule movement into clear decisions for senior stakeholders
Why this one is worth a look
This is a hardware-heavy role, but it is still squarely about getting a robot product from definition to a reliable launch. Agility is already deploying Digit into logistics and manufacturing environments, so the useful question here is not just whether the robot works, but whether the organization can repeatedly turn new platform decisions into field-ready systems.

text:
Staff/Lead Machine Learning Engineer, Behavior and Planning — Nuro — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
User Research
Staff/Lead Machine Learning Engineer, Behavior and Planning
Lead ML work on prediction, decision making, and planning for Nuro's autonomous driving behavior.
What the role actually is
Nuro is hiring a staff or lead ML engineer for Behavior and Planning. The role owns technical leadership on models that shape how the Nuro Driver predicts, decides, plans, and generalizes across new geographies and vehicle platforms.
The posting calls out foundation and world models, LLM/VLM reasoning, reinforcement and imitation learning, diffusion models, and transformer-based prediction and planning. The important part is that the work is meant to move from research ideas onto real vehicles.
What you would work on
Lead ML initiatives across prediction, decision making, and planning
Train and productionize models for safe, natural driving behavior
Build behavior systems that generalize across cities and vehicle platforms
Partner with perception, simulation, evaluation, ML infrastructure, and autonomy teams
What they are asking for
Senior technical leadership experience building and deploying ML systems
Strong ML foundations across model architectures, training, and evaluation
Background in robotics, AI, machine learning, or related technical fields
Experience with sequential decision making, prediction, generative modeling, or reinforcement learning
Why this one is worth a look
Behavior and planning is where autonomy becomes legible to people on the road. This role is worth watching because it joins frontier ML methods with the messy product question of whether a robot's choices feel safe, predictable, and scalable.

text:

User Research
Staff, ML Research Scientist
Research and deploy ML models that help Boston Dynamics robots operate safely around people.
What the role actually is
Boston Dynamics is hiring a staff ML research scientist for its Machine Learning Safety R&D team. The role is about models that help robots detect hazards, understand humans and environmental features, and behave more safely in shared spaces.
For this board, the relevance is the human-aware robotics angle: the work connects ML architecture choices to how robots operate around people.
What you would work on
Research model architectures for robots operating safely near people
Build and validate ML models for hazards, humans, and environmental understanding
Develop datasets, metrics, and validation plans for safety-focused ML research
Prototype perception and behavior models with a small cross-functional team
Carry models through research, deployment, and online validation loops
What they are asking for
Deep learning experience on scalable real-world computer vision, LLM, or robotics problems
Experience across the ML lifecycle from network design to deployment and validation
Familiarity with modern architectures such as transformers, VLMs, VLAs, or deep reinforcement learning
Ability to connect research choices to real robotic safety requirements
Eligibility to work in the United States
Why this one is worth a look
Safety in robotics is often treated as compliance or testing, but this role frames it as a model-design problem. That makes it especially relevant as robots move from controlled workcells into spaces where human behavior is a core part of the environment.

Boston Dynamics

title: Staff Product Manager, Applied AI — Apptronik — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
text:
Staff Product Manager, Applied AI — Apptronik — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
Product
Staff Product Manager, Applied AI
Own the physical AI model roadmap for Apollo, from foundation-model integration to release sequencing.
What the role actually is
Apptronik is hiring a staff product manager for Applied AI on Apollo. The role owns the physical AI model roadmap, including product vision, milestones, release cycles, and how foundation models are integrated, adapted, and fine-tuned into the autonomy stack.
This is a technical product role where the product is not just a user-facing app. It is the model capability stack that determines what the humanoid can do reliably enough to ship.
What you would work on
Own roadmap and release planning for Apollo's physical AI model stack
Sequence foundation-model integration, adaptation, and fine-tuning work
Balance capability velocity against reliability, safety, and product readiness
Partner with engineering, AI, product, and deployment teams on embodied autonomy priorities
What they are asking for
Staff-level product management experience with AI, robotics, autonomy, or complex technical platforms
Ability to turn technical model work into product milestones and release decisions
Comfort working across research, engineering, safety, commercialization, and customer needs
Understanding of foundation models, embodied AI, or robotics autonomy workflows
Why this one is worth a look
As humanoid companies move from demos to product, model capability becomes a roadmap discipline. This role is interesting because it asks a product manager to decide how applied AI work graduates into a robot that customers can actually use.

Apptronik
Austin humanoid robotics company building general-purpose robots for industrial and commercial work.

Staff Product Manager, Platform and Infrastructure — Skydio — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
Product
Staff Product Manager, Platform and Infrastructure
Own Skydio's cloud platform, multi-region infrastructure, compliance capabilities, and on-prem product line.
What the role actually is
Skydio is hiring a staff product manager to own its Cloud Platform and Infrastructure roadmap. The role covers multi-cloud, multi-region, government-compliant platform capabilities and Skydio's on-prem product line for air-gapped and self-hosted deployments.
This is platform product management for autonomous drone customers who need secure, reliable deployments without slowing down operators in the field.
What you would work on
Own the roadmap for Skydio's cloud platform, infrastructure, and deployment capabilities
Productize on-prem, air-gapped, and self-hosted offerings for government and commercial customers
Translate FedRAMP, CJIS, and related requirements into product and operational requirements
Coordinate release scope, launch artifacts, customer pilots, and internal enablement across SRE, cloud, security, legal, GTM, and leadership teams
What they are asking for
Staff-level product judgment for cloud platform, infrastructure, developer-facing, or adjacent technical products
Experience turning customer pain into roadmaps and cross-functional programs
Familiarity with regulated or compliance-shaped product work such as FedRAMP, CJIS, DoD RMF, SOC 2, HIPAA, PCI, or financial controls
Ability to earn engineering trust while translating platform tradeoffs for executives, sales, customers, and auditors
Why this one is worth a look
Robotics companies are becoming infrastructure companies too. Skydio's drones have to operate for public safety, defense, and commercial customers with very different security constraints. This role is about making that deployment complexity feel productized instead of bespoke.

What the role actually is
Skydio is hiring a staff product manager to own telecommunications strategy for its drone platform. The role connects carrier partnerships, regulatory priorities, in-flight data access, business models, and the customer experience of getting a drone connected from first boot.
This is product management for the invisible infrastructure that decides whether autonomous drones can actually operate reliably during real public-safety and commercial missions.
What you would work on
Build Skydio's strategy for telecom-carrier partnerships in the United States and beyond
Turn customer connectivity needs into simple product options and sustainable business models
Set regulatory and carrier-certification priorities for drone connectivity
Monitor usage and costs to validate the economics of in-flight data access
Connect telecom partners with Skydio's field teams for major events and urgent incidents
What they are asking for
Staff-level product judgment for complex customer, partner, or infrastructure products
Experience translating customer needs into priorities and shipped implementation
Ability to build products, partnerships, or business relationships from ambiguous starting points
Comfort working across field teams, carriers, regulators, and internal product groups
Strong communication with both technical and commercial stakeholders
Why this one is worth a look
Connectivity is easy to ignore until a drone needs to stream data during a crowded event or emergency response. This role is interesting because it treats telecom not as procurement, but as a product surface that shapes whether Skydio's autonomous systems are usable in the field.

text:
Staff Research Roboticist — Boston Dynamics — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
User Research
Staff Research Roboticist
Build ML and reinforcement-learning methods that run on Spot for last-mile delivery in outdoor, unstructured environments.
What the role actually is
Boston Dynamics is hiring a staff research roboticist for the Spot team. The role develops learning-based perception and control methods for last-mile delivery, then validates them in simulation and on physical robots.
This is a robotics research role with a direct deployment loop, not a disconnected modeling seat.
What you would work on
Design, train, and deploy ML and reinforcement-learning algorithms for Spot
Test algorithms in simulation and on real robots in unstructured outdoor settings
Build Python and C++ software that can survive hardware integration and field evaluation
Translate research ideas into capabilities for delivery workflows
What they are asking for
Graduate-level robotics, machine learning, computer science, or related background
Experience deploying ML or RL techniques onto physical robotic hardware
Practical depth with modern ML frameworks such as PyTorch, TensorFlow, or JAX
Strong software engineering habits in Python or C++
Why this one is worth a look
Spot delivery work is a useful signal that legged robots are being pushed toward messier logistics tasks outside controlled demos. The caveat is that this is a senior research-and-deployment role: the interesting part is the same thing that makes it hard.

Boston Dynamics
Massachusetts robotics company behind Spot, Stretch, and Atlas, with work spanning mobile manipulation and humanoids.

Collaborative Robotics is hiring a staff-level technical program manager to run software programs for Proxie, its collaborative mobile robot. The role covers autonomy, localization, perception, navigation, robot behaviors, and fleet-management systems.
This is a product-shaped TPM role: the person has to turn customer and deployment needs into executable software plans while keeping engineering, hardware, operations, and leadership aligned.
What you would work on
Lead planning and delivery for robot software and fleet-management programs
Coordinate autonomy, behavior, hardware, operations, and customer-facing dependencies
Translate customer and product needs into technical scope, schedules, and tradeoffs

Ability to work across engineering, product, hardware, operations, and company leadership

Why this one is worth a look
Collaborative Robotics is trying to make robots that fit into human environments instead of forcing the environment to adapt around them. That makes program leadership unusually important: the software roadmap has to connect robot capability, customer workflows, and reliable behavior around people.

Staff Technical Program Manager, V-BAT

Systems-engineering fluency around requirements, interfaces, verification, validation, test planning, and technical baselines
Ability to communicate technical status, tradeoffs, risks, and decisions to engineering leaders, executives, customers, and external stakeholders

Why this one is worth a look
V-BAT is a fielded autonomous aircraft platform, so the program work has real hardware, software, test, and customer constraints. For someone who likes product-adjacent robotics work but wants to stay close to integration and delivery, this is a high-signal TPM role.

Technical Lead, Evaluation Infrastructure
Lead evaluation infrastructure that turns Nuro's autonomy logs and simulations into release-ready behavior evidence.
What the role actually is
Nuro is hiring a technical lead for the infrastructure behind autonomy evaluation and driverless safety validation. The team builds metrics frameworks, evaluation pipelines, analysis products, and tooling that turn simulation and road logs into evidence for L4 autonomy releases.
This is not a classic UX research job, but it belongs on the board because it is about measuring robot behavior in the world: whether the autonomous driver is ready, why it failed, and what evidence should gate deployment.
What you would work on
Lead technical direction for Nuro's autonomy evaluation infrastructure
Build pipelines and metrics that evaluate simulation and on-road autonomy behavior
Improve tooling that helps autonomy and safety teams understand model performance
Shorten the feedback loop between evaluation results, debugging, and release decisions
What they are asking for
Senior technical leadership in autonomy, robotics, ML infrastructure, simulation, or evaluation systems
Experience building reliable data or analysis platforms for complex technical teams
Ability to define metrics that explain behavior quality and safety readiness
Comfort partnering with autonomy, simulation, AI platform, and systems safety groups
Why this one is worth a look
Evaluation is becoming one of the most important disciplines in physical AI. Nuro's role is a good example: the job is less about producing a demo and more about building the evidence layer that decides whether autonomy is improving enough to ship.

Technical Lead Manager, Autonomy Evaluation and Intelligence

Lead a team working at the boundary of simulation, ML, and real-world autonomy

Experience guiding technical teams through ambiguous research and deployment problems
Comfort working in Mountain View with autonomy, safety, and systems teams
Why this one is worth a look
Robotics hiring often talks about model capability, but evaluation is where the truth shows up. This role is compelling because it focuses on the intelligence-measurement layer that decides whether autonomy is improving in ways people can trust.

Technical Program Manager, Architectural Elements
Run program delivery for Dexterity's Architectural Elements group across robot hardware discovery, sourcing, specs, and design.
What the role actually is
Dexterity is hiring a technical program manager for its Architectural Elements group. The group works on new hardware discovery, sourcing, specification, and design across manipulators, mobility, perception, compute, electromechanical systems, and electronics.
This is not a generic coordination job. The TPM is expected to shape the processes that keep Dexterity's hardware design pipeline moving and make day-to-day engineering decisions that affect new robotic systems used in warehouse automation products.

Establish and improve program processes for new robot hardware development

Program management experience with complex hardware or hardware/software systems

Dexterity builds warehouse robots that have to manipulate real goods in production. This role is worth watching because it sits upstream of the product experience: the hardware platform choices that decide what the robot can reliably do before any workflow or interface is layered on top.

Technical Program Manager, Maritime

What the role actually is
Shield AI is hiring a maritime TPM to integrate its Hivemind autonomy stack onto unmanned surface vessels, with future undersea programs also in scope. The work spans program setup, customer alignment, technical integration, test readiness, and operational deployment.
This is a first-of-kind autonomy integration role. The person would coordinate software, platform integration, labs, ground testing, sea trials, customer priorities, and business-development inputs while keeping scope, schedule, cost, and risk visible.

What they are asking for
Senior experience leading complex engineering programs from concept through production or deployment
Technical understanding of software-enabled systems, autonomy, aerospace, maritime systems, or integrated products
Experience managing scope, schedule, budget, risk, and technical performance in fast-moving programs
Strong stakeholder communication across distributed teams
Preferred experience integrating autonomy or software onto defense platforms
Why this one is worth a look
Maritime autonomy is still early enough that program leaders can shape how the product gets integrated and proven, not just execute an existing playbook. The role is defense-heavy and travel-oriented, but it is squarely in the zone where autonomy strategy becomes deployed capability.

Technical Program Manager
Run operations program work that helps Agility scale deployment of the next generation of Digit.
What the role actually is
Agility Robotics is hiring a technical program manager for operations programs tied to Digit deployment. The role bridges supply chain, manufacturing engineering, production, and quality so the operations organization can support the next generation of the humanoid platform.
This is a product-adjacent program role for someone who likes execution systems, risk tracking, and production ramp readiness.
What you would work on
Run weekly execution check-ins across supply chain, technical operations, and manufacturing
Track commitments, risks, and cross-team actions through closure
Serve as a workstream program manager inside larger efforts such as production ramp readiness and capacity expansion
Maintain Jira, Confluence, Smartsheet, Excel, program hubs, dashboards, and decision logs
Prepare monthly operations program reviews with portfolio health, exceptions, and escalations
Help functional teams adopt a single program-management framework and source of truth
What they are asking for
Technical program management experience in operations, hardware, manufacturing, or robotics environments
Ability to drive cross-functional execution with limited oversight
Strong written status, risk management, escalation, and decision follow-through habits
Comfort working hybrid from Agility's Salem operations center
Why this one is worth a look
This is not a pure product strategy role, but it is close to the make-or-break question for humanoids: whether a company can turn a robot platform into a repeatable deployed product. It pairs well with Agility's already-listed senior operations TPM role for candidates at a different level.

Technical Program Manager - Trust and Safety

What the role actually is
Zipline is hiring a technical program manager in South San Francisco to run privacy and trust programs across product, engineering, legal, security, operations, and commercial teams.
The role sits at the product operations layer of autonomous delivery: turning privacy, security, and consumer rights requirements into technical requirements, workflows, and repeatable operating mechanisms.

Own consumer rights request workflows such as deletion, access, correction, opt-out, and related DSAR processes

Build metrics, playbooks, escalation paths, and operating processes for privacy and trust operations

Technical program management, privacy operations, security program management, compliance operations, or product operations experience
Experience with privacy programs, data retention, deletion workflows, data governance, or consumer rights request systems
Ability to translate legal and compliance requirements into practical technical and operational plans

text:
UX Test Engineer - New Grad — Applied Intuition — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
User Research
UX Test Engineer - New Grad
Validate user journeys, UI behavior, and visual consistency for Applied Intuition's autonomy products.
What the role actually is
Applied Intuition is hiring a new-grad UX test engineer to validate product quality through the lens of user experience. The role focuses on user journeys, edge cases, visual consistency, and UI defects across technical autonomy products.
This is closer to UX validation than classic user research, but it belongs on the board because the listing is explicitly about whether complex tools behave clearly for users.
What you would work on
Design validation scripts around user journeys, edge cases, and visual consistency
Maintain automated UI test coverage for autonomy product surfaces
Partner with UX designers and product managers on requirements and prototypes
Identify, reproduce, and track UI and UX defects through resolution
Use product quality work to improve the experience of technical users
What they are asking for
A bachelor's or master's degree in computer science, HMI, UX design, or a related field
New-grad availability around December 2026
Foundational software testing knowledge, including manual and automated methods
Basic scripting ability in languages such as Python, JavaScript, Java, C, or C++
Understanding of design principles, typography, and responsive layout validation
Why this one is worth a look
Robotics and autonomy tooling often fails in small interaction details: confusing states, unclear errors, and interfaces that only experts can interpret. This role is narrow, but it is a useful early-career opening for someone who wants to work where UX, validation, and autonomy meet.

UX Validation Lead
Build Applied Intuition's UX and HMI validation practice for production-grade autonomy interfaces.
What the role actually is
Applied Intuition is hiring a founding UX Validation Lead to build the bridge between HMI concepts and production software quality. The role defines test strategy, creates validation infrastructure, and develops a team around UX and HMI testing.
This is not a conventional qualitative research role. It is closer to a hands-on validation lead for interfaces where usability, automation, and product reliability all matter because the software is tied to vehicles and autonomy workflows.
What you would work on
Define end-to-end HMI and UX validation methods for Applied's products
Build test approaches and automation infrastructure for interface quality
Turn early HMI concepts into validated production-ready product surfaces
Grow test engineers into domain specialists for UX and HMI validation
Work across design, product, and engineering to close gaps before release
What they are asking for
Experience validating complex user interfaces, HMI systems, or safety-relevant software
Ability to design test strategy and build practical validation infrastructure
Comfort leading hands-on work while developing a team and practice area
Strong collaboration with designers, engineers, product managers, and test specialists
Why this one is worth a look
The most interesting part is the "founding" angle. Applied appears to be formalizing how it proves that autonomy interfaces are understandable and production-ready, which is a useful niche for someone who cares about the gap between UX intent and operational reality.

Product
Vice President of Embodied AI
Lead Apptronik's embodied AI strategy across controls, robot learning, manipulation, VLA models, and autonomy.
What the role actually is
Apptronik is hiring a vice president to lead the embodied AI organization behind Apollo. The role owns AI strategy and a large technical organization spanning real-time controls, whole-body reinforcement learning, dexterous manipulation, VLA post-training, and agentic autonomy.
This is not a pure research seat. The listing frames the mandate around turning those stacks into one coherent system that performs useful work for customers.
What you would work on
Define Apptronik's embodied AI vision and roadmap for Apollo
Lead strategy across learned and classical autonomy components
Align model architecture decisions with product needs and customer deployment goals
Guide data collection strategy for improving humanoid robot behavior
Lead a multi-disciplinary AI, controls, and robotics organization
What they are asking for
Senior leadership experience across embodied AI, robotics, controls, or autonomy
Credibility in robot learning, manipulation, reinforcement learning, VLA models, or related research areas
Practical judgment for shipping physical products, not only publishing research
Ability to connect technical strategy with product roadmap and customer readiness
Experience leading large technical teams through ambiguous autonomy problems
Why this one is worth a look
Humanoid companies increasingly need AI leadership that can choose what becomes product, what stays research, and how the pieces fit together safely. This role is worth tracking because it owns that bridge at Apptronik rather than a narrow subsystem.

text:
World Model Research Scientist - Physical AI — Kodiak — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
User Research
World Model Research Scientist - Physical AI
Research world models for Kodiak's physical AI and autonomous trucking stack.
What the role actually is
Kodiak is hiring a world model research scientist for physical AI in Mountain View. The role points at model-based understanding of driving scenes and autonomy behavior for a self-driving trucking platform.
World models matter because they can change how autonomous systems predict, plan, simulate, and evaluate what happens around them.
What you would work on
Research world-model approaches for autonomous driving and physical AI
Build experiments that connect perception, prediction, planning, and simulation
Evaluate model behavior against real-world autonomy needs
Collaborate with autonomy and product teams on how research informs the driving stack
What they are asking for
Research depth in machine learning, autonomy, robotics, or world models
Experience with large-scale model training, simulation, or embodied AI evaluation
Ability to turn research ideas into working autonomy experiments
Strong communication across research and engineering teams
Why this one is worth a look
Kodiak has a focused autonomous trucking domain rather than a generic robotics platform. That makes the world-model work more grounded: success depends on whether the research improves a vehicle that has to operate in high-stakes logistics environments.
About
Kodiak
Mountain View autonomous trucking company building self-driving software for commercial freight and public-sector ground vehicles.

The Robot Age Academy — Product Design & Robot Deployment — The Robot Age
THE ROBOT AGE ACADEMY
Prepare for a world that works with robots.
Robots are entering workplaces, public spaces, and everyday life. Designing, deploying, and managing these systems requires new skills beyond traditional engineering.
The Robot Age Academy develops practical education for professionals responsible for how robots interact with people and operate in the real world.
Two professional learning pathways. No robotics engineering background required.
Explore Programs
Explore the RXD Framework
Our first Product Design for Robots cohort is planned for February 2027.
A five-week professional learning experience for designers who want to apply their skills to robotics. Learn to design human-robot interactions, communicate robot intent, create physical and digital interfaces, and design for unexpected behavior and failure.

Learn how to prepare organizations for successful commercial robotics deployment. Evaluate operational readiness, workforce training, safety requirements, regulation, insurance, cultural fit, change management, adoption, and measurable business outcomes.
Topics
:
Deployment planning, readiness assessments, risk and safety, regulatory requirements, insurance and liability, employee onboarding, cultural adaptation, operational governance, and ROI.
Final project

Explore RDP Curriculum
The Design Gap
As robots enter human environments, teams need professionals who understand behavior, interaction, accessibility, communication, and recovery from failure.
Robots must do more than perform tasks. People need to understand what robots are doing, what they will do next, and how to respond when something goes wrong.
The Deployment Gap
A technically capable robot is not automatically ready for real-world operations.
Organizations need workforce training, safety planning, regulatory awareness, cultural adaptation, operational governance, and measurable adoption to make robotics deployments sustainable.

Commercial robotics deployment requires more than installing hardware and software.
Employees, operators, managers, and customers need the knowledge and confidence to work alongside robots.
The Robot Age develops vendor-neutral training covering deployment readiness, workforce onboarding, human-robot interaction, operational safety, cultural adaptation, and adoption measurement.
Programs can be adapted for robotics manufacturers, integrators, deployment partners, and organizations introducing robots into their operations.
Discuss Corporate Training
About the Instructor
Developed by Michael Posso
Founder, The Robot Age · Product & Technology Leader · Adjunct Professor
Michael Posso is a technology leader, designer, and educator with more than 15 years of experience in digital products, UX engineering, and enterprise technology.
He teaches undergraduate and graduate courses at the Fashion Institute of Technology and New York Institute of Technology and is pursuing a master's degree in Information Design and Technology at SUNY Polytechnic Institute.
Through The Robot Age, he explores how design, technology, and education can help people understand, interact with, and work alongside robots.
His work brings together product design, human-robot interaction, practical robotics experimentation, and professional education.
Designers, researchers, educators, operations professionals, and business leaders will help determine how robots become part of everyday life.
Build the skills to participate in that future.

REP — Robotics Experience Practitioner — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
Overview
The REP is the foundational credential in the Robot Age certification family. It is built entirely on the Robot Experience Design (RXD) framework — six dimensions for evaluating how humans experience robots in real environments. The programme covers the human side of robotics: not how robots are built, but how they behave, where they break down, and what the people around them need to know to work confidently alongside them. No engineering background required.
Built on
Robot Experience Design (RXD)
Every module, deliverable, and capstone in the REP programme maps directly to the six dimensions of the RXD framework — the original research framework developed by The Robot Age for evaluating how humans experience robots in real environments.

title: REP Curriculum — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
text:
REP Curriculum — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
Who this is for
The REP is designed for professionals who work in, around, or alongside robotic systems — but who are not engineers. If your job involves making decisions about how robots show up in human environments, this curriculum was built for you.
Product Designers & UX Strategists
You design the interfaces, environments, and interactions where robots meet people. RXD gives you a structured evaluation method for those moments.
Operations & Deployment Leads
You manage the rollout. You see what breaks. RXD gives you the language to diagnose experience failures and design recovery protocols.
Business Leaders & Strategists
You approve the budget. RXD gives you a scoring instrument to evaluate deployment readiness before signing off — not after.
Programme structure
Week 1 is live on Zoom. Weeks 2 through 5 are self-paced with one scoped deliverable each. Week 6 is the capstone — a full Robot Readiness Audit scored against all six RXD dimensions. You submit it, get cohort feedback, and earn the REP credential.
Week
Format
RXD Dimension(s)
1
Live Zoom
All six (overview)
2
Self-paced + deliverable
Signal Clarity · Spatial Legibility
3
Self-paced + deliverable
Perceived Presence
4
Self-paced + deliverable
Interaction Fit · Failure Transparency
5
Self-paced + deliverable
Recovery Design
6
Capstone submission
Full RXD (all six)
Curriculum
01
What Is Human Robotics Experience?
Live Zoom · Wednesday 7pm ET
All six (introduction)
The opening session introduces the Robot Experience Design framework and the idea that robotics is a human experience problem, not just an engineering one. You will meet Reachy Mini — a social humanoid desktop robot from Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face — and see the six RXD dimensions applied live. No code. No prerequisites.
Topics covered
—
What RXD is and why it exists
—
The six dimensions: Signal Clarity, Spatial Legibility, Perceived Presence, Failure Transparency, Interaction Fit, Recovery Design
—
How the Robot Experience Score (RES) works as a scoring instrument
—
Live demonstration: scoring Reachy Mini across all six dimensions
—
What a Robot Readiness Audit looks like in practice
Deliverable
None — this is the orientation session. Come with questions.
02
Signal Clarity & Spatial Legibility
Self-paced · ~2.5 hours
Signal Clarity · Spatial Legibility
How robots communicate intent — and how humans read their position in space. This week covers the signals a robot sends (lights, sounds, movement, gaze direction) and the spatial cues that tell people where a robot is going, how close it will get, and whether it is aware of them.
Topics covered
—
Signal types: visual, auditory, kinetic, haptic
—
Signal timing and the cost of ambiguity
—
Proxemics in human-robot interaction: personal space, approach angles, territorial boundaries
—
Spatial legibility: can a bystander predict what this robot is about to do?
—
Case study: consumer robots that signal well vs. ones that don't
Deliverable
Signal audit — select a consumer robot (from the Robot of the Week archive or your own environment) and evaluate its Signal Clarity and Spatial Legibility using the RES rubric. 500–800 words with scored dimensions.
Learning outcomes
—
Identify and categorise the signals a robot uses to communicate intent
—
Evaluate whether a robot's spatial behaviour is legible to bystanders
—
Apply the RES scoring criteria for Signal Clarity and Spatial Legibility
03
Perceived Presence
Self-paced · ~2.5 hours
Perceived Presence
Voice, form, aesthetic, emotional readability — the dimension that determines whether people treat a robot as a tool, a character, or a colleague. This week examines how design choices shape the social register of a robot, and why personality coherence matters more than personality itself.
Topics covered
—
What Perceived Presence is and is not (it is not anthropomorphism)
—
Voice design: tone, pacing, register, and the uncanny valley of synthetic speech
—
Form factor and aesthetic as social signals
—
Emotional readability: can people tell what the robot is "feeling" — and should they?
—
The coherence test: does the robot's voice match its body, its context, and its task?
—
Case study: Reachy Mini's expressive design vs. utilitarian service robots
Deliverable
Persona brief — define a deployment context (retail, healthcare, hospitality, public space, education) and write a Perceived Presence specification for Reachy Mini in that context. Cover tone, form factor considerations, social register, and coherence rationale. 500–800 words.
Learning outcomes
—
Distinguish Perceived Presence from anthropomorphism
—
Evaluate a robot's voice, form, and affect as a coherent design system
—
Write a Perceived Presence specification for a defined deployment context
04
Interaction Fit & Failure Transparency
Self-paced · ~2.5 hours
Interaction Fit · Failure Transparency
Is this the right robot for this task, in this context, for these people? And when it fails — because it will — does it fail honestly? This week pairs two dimensions that are tightly linked in practice: the match between robot capability and deployment context, and the design of failure as an intentional moment rather than an exception.
Topics covered
—
Interaction Fit: matching capability to context, task, and user population
—
Over-promising and under-delivering: the deployment gap
—
Failure Transparency: what the robot communicates when something goes wrong
—
Designing failure states: graceful degradation, honest error signals, and the difference between hiding failure and handling it
—
Escalation design: when should a robot hand off to a human, and how?
—
Case study: robots that fail silently vs. robots that fail well
Deliverable
Failure scenario map — using your Week 3 deployment context, define three realistic failure states and specify the Recovery Design for each. Include: what fails, what the user sees, what the robot communicates, and what happens next. Structured template provided.
Learning outcomes
—
Evaluate whether a robot's capabilities match its deployment context
—
Design failure states as intentional interaction moments
—
Specify escalation and handoff protocols for mixed human-robot environments
05
Recovery Design & Applied Use Cases
Self-paced + Reachy Mini session · ~3 hours
Recovery Design
The final self-paced week synthesises all six dimensions across real deployment verticals — retail, hospitality, healthcare, education, public space. You will write an interaction specification for Reachy Mini. TRA runs your spec on the actual robot and returns footage. You then document the gap between what you designed and what you observed.
Topics covered
—
Recovery Design as a system, not an afterthought
—
Full RXD synthesis: how the six dimensions interact in real deployments
—
Writing an interaction specification: structured prompts, expected behaviour, success criteria
—
Vertical deep dives: how RXD applies differently across industries
—
Observing vs. specifying: what the gap between your design and the robot's behaviour reveals
Deliverable
Interaction spec + observation report — write a structured interaction scenario for Reachy Mini. TRA runs it and sends you the footage. Document the gap between your spec and the observed behaviour. This is the direct preparation for the Week 6 capstone.
Learning outcomes
—
Synthesise all six RXD dimensions into a single deployment evaluation
—
Write a testable interaction specification for a social robot
—
Analyse the gap between designed intent and observed robot behaviour
06
Capstone: Robot Readiness Audit
Capstone submission · peer review
All six
The final deliverable. TRA provides a standardised Reachy Mini session — video footage plus an interaction log. You complete a full Robot Readiness Audit: a scored RES across all six RXD dimensions with written rationale for each score. Submit your RRA, receive cohort feedback, and earn the REP credential and badge.
Topics covered
—
RRA methodology: how to structure a professional audit
—
Scoring discipline: calibrating your RES against the rubric
—
Writing the rationale: evidence-based scoring, not opinion
—
Peer review: reading and giving feedback on a colleague's audit
Deliverable
Completed Robot Readiness Audit (RRA) — full RES scoring across all six RXD dimensions with written rationale. Passing threshold earns the REP credential and Credential.net badge.
Learning outcomes
—
Conduct a complete Robot Readiness Audit on a real robot platform
—
Score all six RXD dimensions using the RES instrument with evidence-based rationale
—
Communicate audit findings to a professional audience
What you will walk away with
—
Describe the architecture and behaviour of a robotic system in plain language — no engineering jargon required
—
Identify the moments where human-robot interaction is most likely to break down
—
Apply the Robot Experience Design framework to evaluate any consumer robot deployment
—
Score a robot across all six RXD dimensions using the Robot Experience Score
—
Design communication, escalation, and recovery protocols for mixed human-robot environments
—
Conduct a professional Robot Readiness Audit
—
Earn the REP credential and badge — issued via Credential.net, shareable on LinkedIn
Your platform
Built around Reachy Mini
Every module uses Reachy Mini — an open-source social humanoid robot developed by Pollen Robotics in partnership with Hugging Face. Reachy Mini is expressive, camera-equipped, voice-capable, and designed for exactly the kind of human-robot interaction this programme evaluates. You do not need to own one. TRA operates the hardware; you analyse the experience.
Open Source
Hugging Face
Expressive Head + Antennas
Camera
4-Mic Array
MuJoCo Simulator Available
The framework behind the curriculum
Robot Experience Design (RXD)
RXD is the original research framework developed by The Robot Age. It defines six dimensions for evaluating how humans experience robots — not how robots are engineered, but how they show up in human environments. The REP curriculum teaches you to apply it. The Robot Experience Score (RES) is the scored instrument. The Robot Readiness Audit (RRA) is the professional application.
Signal Clarity
Spatial Legibility
Perceived Presence
Failure Transparency
Interaction Fit
Recovery Design
Read the RXD White Paper →
Founding Cohort — Limited to 10 Seats
Be one of the first Robotics Experience Practitioners.
The founding cohort gets direct access to the course creator, input on the curriculum as it evolves, and a permanent founding member designation on their credential. This rate will not be repeated.
Founding Cohort Rate
$199
or 2 × $99
General Rate (future cohorts)
$399
Enroll Now →
Payment handled securely via Lemon Squeezy. Credential issued via Credential.net upon completion.
Common questions
Do I need an engineering background?
No. The REP is built specifically for non-engineers — product designers, UX strategists, operations leads, and business decision-makers. If you can evaluate a product experience, you can do this programme.
Do I need to own a robot?
No. TRA operates Reachy Mini. You analyse the footage and interaction data we provide. A MuJoCo simulator is also available if you want to run your own sessions, but it is not required.
How much time should I expect to spend per week?
Approximately 2.5 hours per week for self-paced modules and deliverables. Week 1 (live Zoom) is approximately 90 minutes. Week 6 (capstone) may take 3–4 hours depending on your writing pace.
What do I get when I finish?
The REP credential and a digital badge issued via Credential.net. It is shareable on LinkedIn and verifiable by employers.
What is the RXD white paper?
The Robot Experience Design white paper is the published research document that defines the six dimensions and the scoring methodology. It is available on the Research page and provides the theoretical foundation for everything taught in the REP programme.
Can my employer pay for this?
Yes. TRA can issue an invoice for employer reimbursement. Email mike@therobotage.com.
What happens after REP?
REP is the foundational credential in The Robot Age certification family. Specialist tracks and advanced credentials are in development. Founding cohort members will have early access.

The coherence test: does the robot's voice match its body, its context, and its task?
—
Case study: Reachy Mini's expressive design vs. utilitarian service robots
Deliverable
Persona brief — define a deployment context (retail, healthcare, hospitality, public space, education) and write a Perceived Presence specification for Reachy Mini in that context. Cover tone, form factor considerations, social register, and coherence rationale. 500–800 words.
Learning outcomes
—
Distinguish Perceived Presence from anthropomorphism
—
Evaluate a robot's voice, form, and affect as a coherent design system
—
Write a Perceived Presence specification for a defined deployment context
04
Interaction Fit & Failure Transparency
Self-paced · ~2.5 hours
Interaction Fit · Failure Transparency
Is this the right robot for this task, in this context, for these people? And when it fails — because it will — does it fail honestly? This week pairs two dimensions that are tightly linked in practice: the match between robot capability and deployment context, and the design of failure as an intentional moment rather than an exception.
Topics covered
—
Interaction Fit: matching capability to context, task, and user population
—
Over-promising and under-delivering: the deployment gap
—
Failure Transparency: what the robot communicates when something goes wrong
—
Designing failure states: graceful degradation, honest error signals, and the difference between hiding failure and handling it
—
Escalation design: when should a robot hand off to a human, and how?
—
Case study: robots that fail silently vs. robots that fail well
Deliverable
Failure scenario map — using your Week 3 deployment context, define three realistic failure states and specify the Recovery Design for each. Include: what fails, what the user sees, what the robot communicates, and what happens next. Structured template provided.
Learning outcomes
—
Evaluate whether a robot's capabilities match its deployment context
—
Design failure states as intentional interaction moments
—
Specify escalation and handoff protocols for mixed human-robot environments
05
Recovery Design & Applied Use Cases
Self-paced + Reachy Mini session · ~3 hours
Recovery Design
The final self-paced week synthesises all six dimensions across real deployment verticals — retail, hospitality, healthcare, education, public space. You will write an interaction specification for Reachy Mini. TRA runs your spec on the actual robot and returns footage. You then document the gap between what you designed and what you observed.
Topics covered
—
Recovery Design as a system, not an afterthought
—
Full RXD synthesis: how the six dimensions interact in real deployments
—
Writing an interaction specification: structured prompts, expected behaviour, success criteria
—
Vertical deep dives: how RXD applies differently across industries
—
Observing vs. specifying: what the gap between your design and the robot's behaviour reveals
Deliverable
Interaction spec + observation report — write a structured interaction scenario for Reachy Mini. TRA runs it and sends you the footage. Document the gap between your spec and the observed behaviour. This is the direct preparation for the Week 6 capstone.
Learning outcomes
—
Synthesise all six RXD dimensions into a single deployment evaluation
—
Write a testable interaction specification for a social robot
—
Analyse the gap between designed intent and observed robot behaviour
06
Capstone: Robot Readiness Audit
Capstone submission · peer review
All six
The final deliverable. TRA provides a standardised Reachy Mini session — video footage plus an interaction log. You complete a full Robot Readiness Audit: a scored RES across all six RXD dimensions with written rationale for each score. Submit your RRA, receive cohort feedback, and earn the REP credential and badge.
Topics covered
—
RRA methodology: how to structure a professional audit
—
Scoring discipline: calibrating your RES against the rubric
—
Writing the rationale: evidence-based scoring, not opinion
—
Peer review: reading and giving feedback on a colleague's audit
Deliverable
Completed Robot Readiness Audit (RRA) — full RES scoring across all six RXD dimensions with written rationale. Passing threshold earns the REP credential and Credential.net badge.
Learning outcomes
—
Conduct a complete Robot Readiness Audit on a real robot platform
—
Score all six RXD dimensions using the RES instrument with evidence-based rationale
—
Communicate audit findings to a professional audience
What you will walk away with
—
Describe the architecture and behaviour of a robotic system in plain language — no engineering jargon required
—
Identify the moments where human-robot interaction is most likely to break down
—
Apply the Robot Experience Design framework to evaluate any consumer robot deployment
—
Score a robot across all six RXD dimensions using the Robot Experience Score
—
Design communication, escalation, and recovery protocols for mixed human-robot environments
—
Conduct a professional Robot Readiness Audit
—
Earn the REP credential and badge — issued via Credential.net, shareable on LinkedIn
Your platform
Built around Reachy Mini
Every module uses Reachy Mini — an open-source social humanoid robot developed by Pollen Robotics in partnership with Hugging Face. Reachy Mini is expressive, camera-equipped, voice-capable, and designed for exactly the kind of human-robot interaction this programme evaluates. You do not need to own one. TRA operates the hardware; you analyse the experience.

The framework behind the curriculum
Robot Experience Design (RXD)
RXD is the original research framework developed by The Robot Age. It defines six dimensions for evaluating how humans experience robots — not how robots are engineered, but how they show up in human environments. The REP curriculum teaches you to apply it. The Robot Experience Score (RES) is the scored instrument. The Robot Readiness Audit (RRA) is the professional application.

Common questions
Do I need an engineering background?
No. The REP is built specifically for non-engineers — product designers, UX strategists, operations leads, and business decision-makers. If you can evaluate a product experience, you can do this programme.
Do I need to own a robot?
No. TRA operates Reachy Mini. You analyse the footage and interaction data we provide. A MuJoCo simulator is also available if you want to run your own sessions, but it is not required.
How much time should I expect to spend per week?
Approximately 2.5 hours per week for self-paced modules and deliverables. Week 1 (live Zoom) is approximately 90 minutes. Week 6 (capstone) may take 3–4 hours depending on your writing pace.
What do I get when I finish?
The REP credential and a digital badge issued via Credential.net. It is shareable on LinkedIn and verifiable by employers.
What is the RXD white paper?
The Robot Experience Design white paper is the published research document that defines the six dimensions and the scoring methodology. It is available on the Research page and provides the theoretical foundation for everything taught in the REP programme.
Can my employer pay for this?
Yes. TRA can issue an invoice for employer reimbursement. Email mike@therobotage.com.
What happens after REP?
REP is the foundational credential in The Robot Age certification family. Specialist tracks and advanced credentials are in development. Founding cohort members will have early access.

Operations & Deployment Leads
You manage the rollout. You see what breaks. RXD gives you the language to diagnose experience failures and design recovery protocols.
Business Leaders & Strategists
You approve the budget. RXD gives you a scoring instrument to evaluate deployment readiness before signing off — not after.

Week 1 is live on Zoom. Weeks 2 through 5 are self-paced with one scoped deliverable each. Week 6 is the capstone — a full Robot Readiness Audit scored against all six RXD dimensions. You submit it, get cohort feedback, and earn the REP credential.

Signal Clarity · Spatial Legibility

Signal types: visual, auditory, kinetic, haptic

Signal timing and the cost of ambiguity

Form factor and aesthetic as social signals

—
Distinguish Perceived Presence from anthropomorphism
—

Write a Perceived Presence specification for a defined deployment context

Specify escalation and handoff protocols for mixed human-robot environments

· Curriculum
Six weeks. Six dimensions. One framework.
The REP programme walks you through the Robot Experience Design framework dimension by dimension — from how robots signal intent to how they recover from failure. Every week builds on the last. Every deliverable is scoped to a real robot.

~15 Hours Total
1 Live Zoom + Async

Who this is for
The REP is designed for professionals who work in, around, or alongside robotic systems — but who are not engineers. If your job involves making decisions about how robots show up in human environments, this curriculum was built for you.
Product Designers & UX Strategists
You design the interfaces, environments, and interactions where robots meet people. RXD gives you a structured evaluation method for those moments.
Operations & Deployment Leads
You manage the rollout. You see what breaks. RXD gives you the language to diagnose experience failures and design recovery protocols.
Business Leaders & Strategists
You approve the budget. RXD gives you a scoring instrument to evaluate deployment readiness before signing off — not after.
Programme structure
Week 1 is live on Zoom. Weeks 2 through 5 are self-paced with one scoped deliverable each. Week 6 is the capstone — a full Robot Readiness Audit scored against all six RXD dimensions. You submit it, get cohort feedback, and earn the REP credential.
