Curriculum
01
What Is Human Robotics Experience?
Live Zoom · Wednesday 7pm ET
All six (introduction)
The opening session introduces the Robot Experience Design framework and the idea that robotics is a human experience problem, not just an engineering one. You will meet Reachy Mini — a social humanoid desktop robot from Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face — and see the six RXD dimensions applied live. No code. No prerequisites.
Topics covered
—
What RXD is and why it exists
—
The six dimensions: Signal Clarity, Spatial Legibility, Perceived Presence, Failure Transparency, Interaction Fit, Recovery Design
—
How the Robot Experience Score (RES) works as a scoring instrument
—
Live demonstration: scoring Reachy Mini across all six dimensions
—
What a Robot Readiness Audit looks like in practice
Deliverable
None — this is the orientation session. Come with questions.
02
Signal Clarity & Spatial Legibility
Self-paced · ~2.5 hours
Signal Clarity · Spatial Legibility
How robots communicate intent — and how humans read their position in space. This week covers the signals a robot sends (lights, sounds, movement, gaze direction) and the spatial cues that tell people where a robot is going, how close it will get, and whether it is aware of them.
Topics covered
—
Signal types: visual, auditory, kinetic, haptic
—
Signal timing and the cost of ambiguity
—
Proxemics in human-robot interaction: personal space, approach angles, territorial boundaries
—
Spatial legibility: can a bystander predict what this robot is about to do?
—
Case study: consumer robots that signal well vs. ones that don't
Deliverable
Signal audit — select a consumer robot (from the Robot of the Week archive or your own environment) and evaluate its Signal Clarity and Spatial Legibility using the RES rubric. 500–800 words with scored dimensions.
Learning outcomes
—
Identify and categorise the signals a robot uses to communicate intent
—
Evaluate whether a robot's spatial behaviour is legible to bystanders
—
Apply the RES scoring criteria for Signal Clarity and Spatial Legibility
03
Perceived Presence
Self-paced · ~2.5 hours
Perceived Presence
Voice, form, aesthetic, emotional readability — the dimension that determines whether people treat a robot as a tool, a character, or a colleague. This week examines how design choices shape the social register of a robot, and why personality coherence matters more than personality itself.
Topics covered
—
What Perceived Presence is and is not (it is not anthropomorphism)
—
Voice design: tone, pacing, register, and the uncanny valley of synthetic speech
—
Form factor and aesthetic as social signals
—
Emotional readability: can people tell what the robot is "feeling" — and should they?
—
The coherence test: does the robot's voice match its body, its context, and its task?
—
Case study: Reachy Mini's expressive design vs. utilitarian service robots
Deliverable
Persona brief — define a deployment context (retail, healthcare, hospitality, public space, education) and write a Perceived Presence specification for Reachy Mini in that context. Cover tone, form factor considerations, social register, and coherence rationale. 500–800 words.
Learning outcomes
—
Distinguish Perceived Presence from anthropomorphism
—
Evaluate a robot's voice, form, and affect as a coherent design system
—
Write a Perceived Presence specification for a defined deployment context
04
Interaction Fit & Failure Transparency
Self-paced · ~2.5 hours
Interaction Fit · Failure Transparency
Is this the right robot for this task, in this context, for these people? And when it fails — because it will — does it fail honestly? This week pairs two dimensions that are tightly linked in practice: the match between robot capability and deployment context, and the design of failure as an intentional moment rather than an exception.
Topics covered
—
Interaction Fit: matching capability to context, task, and user population
—
Over-promising and under-delivering: the deployment gap
—
Failure Transparency: what the robot communicates when something goes wrong
—
Designing failure states: graceful degradation, honest error signals, and the difference between hiding failure and handling it
—
Escalation design: when should a robot hand off to a human, and how?
—
Case study: robots that fail silently vs. robots that fail well
Deliverable
Failure scenario map — using your Week 3 deployment context, define three realistic failure states and specify the Recovery Design for each. Include: what fails, what the user sees, what the robot communicates, and what happens next. Structured template provided.
Learning outcomes
—
Evaluate whether a robot's capabilities match its deployment context
—
Design failure states as intentional interaction moments
—
Specify escalation and handoff protocols for mixed human-robot environments
05
Recovery Design & Applied Use Cases
Self-paced + Reachy Mini session · ~3 hours
Recovery Design
The final self-paced week synthesises all six dimensions across real deployment verticals — retail, hospitality, healthcare, education, public space. You will write an interaction specification for Reachy Mini. TRA runs your spec on the actual robot and returns footage. You then document the gap between what you designed and what you observed.
Topics covered
—
Recovery Design as a system, not an afterthought
—
Full RXD synthesis: how the six dimensions interact in real deployments
—
Writing an interaction specification: structured prompts, expected behaviour, success criteria
—
Vertical deep dives: how RXD applies differently across industries
—
Observing vs. specifying: what the gap between your design and the robot's behaviour reveals
Deliverable
Interaction spec + observation report — write a structured interaction scenario for Reachy Mini. TRA runs it and sends you the footage. Document the gap between your spec and the observed behaviour. This is the direct preparation for the Week 6 capstone.
Learning outcomes
—
Synthesise all six RXD dimensions into a single deployment evaluation
—
Write a testable interaction specification for a social robot
—
Analyse the gap between designed intent and observed robot behaviour
06
Capstone: Robot Readiness Audit
Capstone submission · peer review
All six
The final deliverable. TRA provides a standardised Reachy Mini session — video footage plus an interaction log. You complete a full Robot Readiness Audit: a scored RES across all six RXD dimensions with written rationale for each score. Submit your RRA, receive cohort feedback, and earn the REP credential and badge.
Topics covered
—
RRA methodology: how to structure a professional audit
—
Scoring discipline: calibrating your RES against the rubric
—
Writing the rationale: evidence-based scoring, not opinion
—
Peer review: reading and giving feedback on a colleague's audit
Deliverable
Completed Robot Readiness Audit (RRA) — full RES scoring across all six RXD dimensions with written rationale. Passing threshold earns the REP credential and Credential.net badge.
Learning outcomes
—
Conduct a complete Robot Readiness Audit on a real robot platform
—
Score all six RXD dimensions using the RES instrument with evidence-based rationale
—
Communicate audit findings to a professional audience

title: Agility's Digit 5 bet is that legs can become a business model — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
text:
Agility's Digit 5 bet is that legs can become a business model — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
ANALYSIS
October 9, 2026
The Robot Age Editorial Team
Agility's Digit 5 bet is that legs can become a business model
Agility Robotics has the thing most humanoid companies still want: proof that a bipedal robot has done real work in real industrial facilities.
That does not mean the business case is proven. It means the question has changed. Digit is no longer only a robot-design story. It is now an economics story.
Agility's latest SPAC materials with Churchill Capital Corp XI describe a company trying to convert real deployments, a new generation of hardware, and more than $300 million in multi-year Digit 5 orders into a scaled humanoid business. The pitch is direct: Digit 4 proved that a humanoid can work in logistics and manufacturing environments;
Digit 5
is supposed to prove that a humanoid can scale.
That is the right test. The humanoid race is no longer about whether a robot can walk on video. It is about whether the robot can earn its keep.
The business is still early
Agility is going public around a large future narrative. The proposed deal values the company at a $2.5 billion pre-money equity value and is expected to provide more than $620 million in gross proceeds, according to the
June 2026 Churchill investor presentation filed with the SEC
.
The same materials emphasize real traction: nine committed customer facility deployments, 65,000 hours of operations, a RoboFab facility designed for 10,000 robots per year, and more than $300 million in committed Digit 5 orders. But those orders are not current revenue. The footnote matters: Agility says the order figure reflects expected multi-year value, subject to contractual milestones, and relates to a 1,000-robot, three-year RaaS contract.
The Robot Report
later highlighted the gap between the ambition and the current base: Agility generated $1.8 million in 2025 net sales against a $140 million operating loss, with roughly $100 million of cash burn. That is not unusual for a company trying to industrialize a new robotics category. But it is the whole story: Agility has evidence. It does not yet have scale.
The SPAC is therefore not a celebration lap. It is fuel for the harder phase: manufacturing, deployment density, service cost, customer retention, and repeatable ROI.
Digit 5 changes the economic argument
Digit 5 is the robot Agility wants investors and customers to underwrite.
The upgrade is not cosmetic. Agility says Digit 5 is built for "cooperatively safe" work near people, using human detection, safety cues, and independent safe motion control to reduce reliance on traditional guarding. It also claims a 50 lb payload, a 90-minute battery that charges in nine minutes, a 10:1 run-to-charge ratio, swappable end-effectors, a 5'11" human-scale body, and a 7.2-foot reach.
Those specs matter because they broaden the economic surface area. Digit 4 has mostly been associated with tote handling. Digit 5 is being positioned for decanting, palletizing and depalletizing, machine tending, kitting, sequencing, inspection, and broader material flow.
That is the bet: the robot becomes more valuable when it is not a single-purpose machine. If one humanoid body can learn more workflows over time, the customer does not have to buy a new fixed automation cell for each task. Agility keeps the same basic robot, adds skills through software, and captures more lifetime value through Agility Arc, deployment services, maintenance, and fleet expansion.
In the investor deck, Agility frames two adoption models:
Robots-as-a-Service:
roughly $8,500 per month, or about $100,000 per year, plus a deployment fee, producing about $500,000 in illustrative revenue to Agility over a five-year useful life.
Ownership plus software and maintenance:
upfront robot purchase, deployment fee, and recurring services, producing about $400,000 in illustrative revenue over five years.
Those numbers are not guarantees. The filing says they are illustrative, built on management assumptions. But they show what Agility needs Digit 5 to become: not a one-time hardware sale, but an industrial asset with recurring software, support, and workflow value.
The customer math is simple and fragile
Agility's customer case is built against labor. The SEC presentation compares Digit 5 to a fully burdened human labor cost of about $30.50 per hour, across two 10-hour shifts per day, 120 hours per week. Under that model, the company argues that a $100,000 annual RaaS cost can replace about $200,000 of annual labor value and create roughly $100,000 of annual customer savings.
That is a clean slide. Real facilities are messier.
The savings only appear if Digit is assigned to work that actually needs those hours, if it stays productive, if it does not introduce too much supervision or recovery overhead, if service costs stay controlled, and if the customer can reorganize workflow around the robot. A humanoid that works well for a tightly scoped tote path is valuable. A humanoid that must be babysat, fenced off, frequently reset, or limited to one narrow task becomes expensive very quickly.
This is why the deployment evidence matters more than the headline valuation.
Agility says Digit has more than 65,000 hours of real-world operation and work across customer sites including GXO, Schaeffler, Amazon, and Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada. At GXO's Flowery Branch facility near Atlanta, Agility says Digit 4 reached a 100,000-tote milestone with about 98% on-task accuracy. Agility also describes
Digit's GXO deployment
as a long-term commercial role in a facility near Atlanta.
That is the most important part of the Agility story. Not the humanoid shape. Not the SPAC. The hours.
The real U.S. deployment story is still concentrated
The most concrete U.S. deployment is GXO. In 2024, GXO and Agility announced a multi-year agreement to deploy Digit in GXO logistics operations after a proof-of-concept pilot, with the first live work tied to a Spanx facility in Georgia.
GXO's announcement
described Digit robots and Agility Arc working under a RaaS model, coordinating tasks such as moving totes from cobots to conveyors.
That is real deployment, but it is not yet a broad labor replacement story. It is a narrow industrial workflow where the value proposition is easier to test: repetitive material movement, known facility layout, controlled handoffs, measurable throughput, and existing automation islands that need connection.
Amazon is the more complicated signal. Agility lists Amazon among its customers and strategic investors, and Digit has been tested in Amazon-linked contexts. But Amazon is also one of the world's most sophisticated builders and operators of warehouse automation. If Amazon is learning from Digit, that is validation. It is also a reminder that the buyer may eventually want internal leverage, not dependency.
Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada and Schaeffler add industrial credibility. They suggest the use case is not only e-commerce totes. But the publicly visible pattern is still early: pilots, facility-specific deployments, and a narrow set of repetitive work.
That should not be held against Agility. This is how serious robots enter the world. The danger is treating the first commercial deployments as if they already prove mass adoption.
Why bipedal is the strategy, not the stunt
The easy critique is that wheels are cheaper. Most of the time, they are. Warehouses already use AMRs, conveyors, arms, shuttles, lifts, and fixed automation. A bipedal robot carries all the complexity of balance, gait, foot placement, actuation, fall risk, safety validation, and whole-body control.
So why bet the company on legs?
Because Agility is not trying to build the cheapest way to move one object along one path. It is trying to build a robot body that can enter environments designed for people without the facility being rebuilt around the robot. That is the strategic case for a humanoid biped:
Human-scale access:
Digit can work around shelves, totes, conveyors, aisles, carts, pallets, doorways, and workstations built for people.
Vertical reach:
A human-height body can interact with the built environment without every handoff being redesigned.
Workflow flexibility:
A walking, lifting, reaching machine can theoretically move between tasks as software skills improve.
Deployment density:
If one platform can cover more jobs at a site over time, the customer can expand within a facility instead of buying a separate automation island for each workflow.
Labor substitutability:
The humanoid form maps directly to jobs already written around human motion, even if the robot is not humanlike in intelligence.
That is Agility's central insight: the humanoid is not just a marketing shape. It is a compatibility layer for a world already built at human scale.
The risk is that compatibility is expensive. If a wheeled robot can do the same job, the biped loses. If fixed automation can do the same job more reliably, the biped loses. If the humanoid's extra mobility does not create enough additional workflow coverage, the economics compress.
Agility's strategy only works if legs unlock enough useful work to justify their complexity.
The manufacturing challenge is the business challenge
Agility's RoboFab facility in Salem, Oregon is designed for up to 10,000 robots per year at full capacity. The investor deck also says roughly 75% of Digit parts are sourced from the U.S. That matters in a world where robotics is increasingly tied to supply-chain resilience, defense-adjacent policy, and industrial sovereignty.
But a factory designed for 10,000 units is not the same thing as a factory producing 10,000 useful, serviceable, margin-positive robots.
The SEC materials make the manufacturing risk explicit. Agility says it has limited experience commercializing Digit at scale and no experience in high-volume manufacturing. It also warns that Digit 5 remains in development and that customer orders are subject to milestones. Those are not throwaway legal lines. They are the main risks.
Humanoid robots are mechanically intense products. Cost down is not automatic. Batteries, actuators, sensors, compute, safety systems, service parts, field support, reliability testing, and customer-specific integration all fight the margin story. Agility's deck shows a path to lower bill-of-material costs as volume rises, but the word "path" is doing a lot of work.
Digit 5 will be judged by boring metrics: uptime, failures per shift, service response, parts cost, deployment time, human supervision burden, customer renewal, and expansion per site.
The Robot Age view
Agility's strategy is coherent. That is the strongest thing to say about it.
The company is not selling a general-purpose household fantasy first. It is selling a bipedal industrial body into places where human-scale movement still matters: warehouses, logistics sites, factories, and material-flow environments with repetitive work and labor pressure. It has real deployments. It has a factory. It has a cloud fleet layer. It has a new robot designed around safer work near people. It has customers willing to sign orders if milestones are met.
But the economics are still a bet. The current revenue base is tiny compared with the valuation and the deployment targets. The order book is not revenue. The RaaS model depends on utilization. The ownership model depends on customers believing a humanoid can retain value over a five-year life. The whole strategy depends on Digit 5 turning bipedal complexity into facility-level flexibility.
That makes Agility one of the most interesting humanoid companies precisely because it is past the demo phase and not yet past the proof phase.
Digit 5 is not a victory lap. It is the first serious test of whether legs can be more than a spectacle.
If Agility is right, the humanoid robot becomes an adaptable labor platform for spaces already built around humans. If Agility is wrong, Digit becomes an expensive reminder that looking compatible with human work is not the same as being economically deployable.
That is the real SPAC question. Not whether humanoids are coming. Whether one of them can finally pay for its legs.

title: America's first humanoid IPO arrives — China's already turned a profit — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
text:
America's first humanoid IPO arrives — China's already turned a profit — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
NEWS
June 25, 2026
The Robot Age Editorial Team
America's first humanoid IPO arrives — China's already turned a profit
Agility Robotics will become the first company on a US exchange built entirely to make and sell humanoid robots. On June 24, 2026 the Oregon-based maker of Digit announced a merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a special-purpose acquisition company, at a $2.5 billion valuation, with shares set to trade under the ticker AGLT. It is not the only humanoid company reaching public markets this year — and it is not the most profitable.
What Agility is selling, and where it runs
Agility is going public on contracted demand, not a pitch deck. The company reports more than $300 million in multi-year orders for its next-generation Digit v5 and a pipeline of over 30 customers. The deal brings roughly $620 million in gross proceeds — $420 million in cash from Churchill XI plus more than $200 million in a placement led by Foxconn — earmarked for fulfilling orders and scaling Digit v5 production.
Those orders are grounded in real US deployments. Digit runs eight-hour daily shifts at Schaeffler's plant in Cheraw, South Carolina, and has moved more than 100,000 totes at GXO's warehouse in Flowery Branch, Georgia, since June 2024. Across nine customer facilities, Digit has logged more than 65,000 operating hours in live production environments — the number that distinguishes Agility from most of the field.
Digit, Agility's flagship humanoid. Image: Agility Robotics
Flagship robot model
Digit
Agility Robotics · Salem, Oregon
A bipedal, human-centric robot built for warehouse and factory work — it walks, climbs stairs, and moves totes and packages alongside people.
Height
175 cm (5 ft 9 in)
Weight
~76 kg (168 lb)
Payload
16 kg (35 lb)
Walking speed
1.5 m/s (3.1 mph)
Runtime
4+ hours per charge
Degrees of freedom
16
Sensing
LiDAR + depth cameras
Fleet platform
Agility Arc (cloud)
Status
Commercially deployed; 65,000+ operating hours
The American humanoid that isn't listing
Figure AI is the comparison that explains the bet. The California company raised more than $1 billion last September at a $39 billion post-money valuation — more than fifteen times Agility's — backed by Intel Capital, Salesforce, Qualcomm Ventures, and Bezos Expeditions. It has filed no S-1; market consensus puts any listing in 2027 or 2028.
Figure has its own US deployment to point to. At BMW's plant in Spartanburg, South Carolina, its Figure 02 robot worked ten-hour shifts for ten months, loading more than 90,000 sheet-metal parts across roughly 1,250 operating hours and contributing to over 30,000 X3 vehicles at better than 99% placement accuracy. A $39 billion private valuation rests on that single line of factory evidence; Agility is going public on far more deployment hours at a sixteenth of the price.
China already did it — profitably
Unitree beat both to a public market. On June 1, 2026 Shanghai's STAR Market cleared the Chinese company's listing — the first "embodied AI" IPO on China's A-share market — targeting a valuation near 42 billion yuan, about $6.2 billion, and raising roughly $608 million. The difference that matters: Unitree makes money.
Unitree posted 2025 revenue of about 1.7 billion yuan (
$236 million) and adjusted net profit near 591 million yuan (
$82 million), at a gross margin around 60%. It shipped more than 5,500 humanoids in 2025 — first in the world by unit volume, roughly a third of the market — and is scaling toward 20,000 in 2026. Its products sell on price: the G1 starts near $13,500, the H2 lists at $29,900, the flagship H1 runs about $90,000.
The numbers don't line up
Three companies are building the same machine and the market prices them from $2.5 billion to $39 billion. Agility sells a small number of expensive enterprise robots on multi-year contracts, measured in operating hours. Unitree sells thousands of cheaper units to labs, developers, and factories, measured in shipments and profit. Figure sells a valuation and a BMW pilot. Humanoid revenue went from under 2% of Unitree's sales in 2023 to more than half by late 2025 — a commercial curve neither US company can yet show.
A rounding error in the year of the mega-IPO
Set against 2026's headline listings, both humanoid IPOs vanish. SpaceX has already gone public, raising $85.7 billion near a $1.8 trillion valuation. OpenAI is moving toward a September listing targeting $852 billion to $1 trillion. Anthropic, which raised $65 billion at a $965 billion valuation, crossed a $44 billion revenue run-rate in May. Together the three target roughly $3.6 trillion — the GDP of France. Goldman Sachs projects $160 billion in total 2026 IPO proceeds; Agility and Unitree combined are a footnote to it.
The two humanoid companies ringing bells in 2026 are doing it on opposite logic — one on contracted hours, the other on shipped units and a profit it can already book. Whether public markets reward either of them over the trillion-dollar AI narratives is the test embodied robotics just walked into.

June 25, 2026
The Robot Age Editorial Team
America's first humanoid IPO arrives — China's already turned a profit
Agility Robotics will become the first company on a US exchange built entirely to make and sell humanoid robots. On June 24, 2026 the Oregon-based maker of Digit announced a merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a special-purpose acquisition company, at a $2.5 billion valuation, with shares set to trade under the ticker AGLT. It is not the only humanoid company reaching public markets this year — and it is not the most profitable.
What Agility is selling, and where it runs
Agility is going public on contracted demand, not a pitch deck. The company reports more than $300 million in multi-year orders for its next-generation Digit v5 and a pipeline of over 30 customers. The deal brings roughly $620 million in gross proceeds — $420 million in cash from Churchill XI plus more than $200 million in a placement led by Foxconn — earmarked for fulfilling orders and scaling Digit v5 production.
Those orders are grounded in real US deployments. Digit runs eight-hour daily shifts at Schaeffler's plant in Cheraw, South Carolina, and has moved more than 100,000 totes at GXO's warehouse in Flowery Branch, Georgia, since June 2024. Across nine customer facilities, Digit has logged more than 65,000 operating hours in live production environments — the number that distinguishes Agility from most of the field.
Digit, Agility's flagship humanoid. Image: Agility Robotics

The American humanoid that isn't listing
Figure AI is the comparison that explains the bet. The California company raised more than $1 billion last September at a $39 billion post-money valuation — more than fifteen times Agility's — backed by Intel Capital, Salesforce, Qualcomm Ventures, and Bezos Expeditions. It has filed no S-1; market consensus puts any listing in 2027 or 2028.
Figure has its own US deployment to point to. At BMW's plant in Spartanburg, South Carolina, its Figure 02 robot worked ten-hour shifts for ten months, loading more than 90,000 sheet-metal parts across roughly 1,250 operating hours and contributing to over 30,000 X3 vehicles at better than 99% placement accuracy. A $39 billion private valuation rests on that single line of factory evidence; Agility is going public on far more deployment hours at a sixteenth of the price.
China already did it — profitably
Unitree beat both to a public market. On June 1, 2026 Shanghai's STAR Market cleared the Chinese company's listing — the first "embodied AI" IPO on China's A-share market — targeting a valuation near 42 billion yuan, about $6.2 billion, and raising roughly $608 million. The difference that matters: Unitree makes money.
Unitree posted 2025 revenue of about 1.7 billion yuan (
$236 million) and adjusted net profit near 591 million yuan (
$82 million), at a gross margin around 60%. It shipped more than 5,500 humanoids in 2025 — first in the world by unit volume, roughly a third of the market — and is scaling toward 20,000 in 2026. Its products sell on price: the G1 starts near $13,500, the H2 lists at $29,900, the flagship H1 runs about $90,000.
The numbers don't line up
Three companies are building the same machine and the market prices them from $2.5 billion to $39 billion. Agility sells a small number of expensive enterprise robots on multi-year contracts, measured in operating hours. Unitree sells thousands of cheaper units to labs, developers, and factories, measured in shipments and profit. Figure sells a valuation and a BMW pilot. Humanoid revenue went from under 2% of Unitree's sales in 2023 to more than half by late 2025 — a commercial curve neither US company can yet show.
A rounding error in the year of the mega-IPO
Set against 2026's headline listings, both humanoid IPOs vanish. SpaceX has already gone public, raising $85.7 billion near a $1.8 trillion valuation. OpenAI is moving toward a September listing targeting $852 billion to $1 trillion. Anthropic, which raised $65 billion at a $965 billion valuation, crossed a $44 billion revenue run-rate in May. Together the three target roughly $3.6 trillion — the GDP of France. Goldman Sachs projects $160 billion in total 2026 IPO proceeds; Agility and Unitree combined are a footnote to it.
The two humanoid companies ringing bells in 2026 are doing it on opposite logic — one on contracted hours, the other on shipped units and a profit it can already book. Whether public markets reward either of them over the trillion-dollar AI narratives is the test embodied robotics just walked into.

title: Atlas turned halftime into an interface test — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
text:
Atlas turned halftime into an interface test — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
NEWS
July 8, 2026
The Robot Age Editorial Team
Atlas turned halftime into an interface test
Atlas at the World Cup was a public interface test for humanoid robots. On July 5, Hyundai Motor Company brought Boston Dynamics' Atlas into the FIFA World Cup 2026 Round of 16 match at New York/New Jersey Stadium, where the robot performed football-inspired movements and delivered the ceremonial match ball to the referee.
The company framed the moment as the
first robotics-powered halftime activation
on football's biggest stage. It also marked the first public demonstration of the production version of Atlas' real-world movement capabilities after its CES 2026 introduction. That matters because the setting was not a lab, a conference stage, or a controlled product video. It was a live sports environment built around timing, crowd attention, broadcast framing, and no tolerance for awkward ambiguity.
The choreography was the product
Atlas performed goal celebrations inspired by Harry Kane, Erling Haaland, Matheus Cunha, and Son Heung-min before handing the ball to the referee. For a brand activation, that reads as spectacle. For robotics teams, it reads as a choreography problem: the robot had to be expressive enough for the crowd, bounded enough for the field, and predictable enough for every human standing near it.
Hyundai said the performance used retargeting technology, reinforcement learning, and whole-body control. Retargeting translated human movements into Atlas' form. Reinforcement learning refined those movements through simulation. Whole-body control coordinated the motion across the robot's body. Those are not only demo techniques. Boston Dynamics' director of robotics behavior, Alberto Rodriguez, said the training approach was similar to how the company teaches Atlas real-world industrial applications.
Public robots need readable intent
The useful design question is not whether Atlas looked impressive. The question is whether people could read what it was doing before it did it. A stadium robot has to make its path, posture, handoff, pause, and exit legible at a glance. The same is true in a warehouse aisle, factory cell, hospital corridor, or retail back room.
That is where the World Cup appearance becomes more than a marketing moment. Humanoid robots will not earn trust only by lifting weight or balancing well. They will earn it through timing, spatial courtesy, failure signals, and recoverable movement around people who did not opt into a robotics demo.
The factory story was hiding under the halftime story
Boston Dynamics positions
Atlas
as an enterprise humanoid for industrial work, especially material handling. The product page lists barcode scanning, workflow integrations, autonomous navigation to a charging station, self-swappable batteries, four hours of battery life, 56 degrees of freedom, a 2.3-meter reach, and load capacity up to 50 kg instant or 30 kg sustained. It also says Atlas is taking its first steps into a Hyundai customer facility for field testing on real-world sequencing tasks.
Atlas at FIFA World Cup 2026. Image: Hyundai Motor Group / Boston Dynamics

That makes the World Cup activation a public-facing version of the same core problem. In the stadium, Atlas had to move a ball, perform a social script, and share space with humans under broadcast pressure. In a plant, the tasks will be less theatrical but more consequential: part sequencing, machine tending, order building, handoffs, charging, escalation, and fleet oversight.
Brand trust is part of deployment readiness
Hyundai's role as Official Robotics Partner matters because it turned Atlas from a robotics-company artifact into a mainstream brand encounter. Most people will meet humanoids first through moments like this: a halftime appearance, a retail pilot, a hotel lobby, an airport corridor, a facility tour. Those encounters will shape expectations before the robot ever enters a job site.
For designers and product managers, the lesson is practical. A humanoid deployment is never only a capability problem. It is also a legibility problem, a choreography problem, and a trust problem. Atlas did not prove that humanoids are ready for ordinary public life. It showed how much interface work has to happen before ordinary people can stand near one without needing an explanation.

title: Automation anxiety vs. automation readiness: what the data actually shows — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
text:
Automation anxiety vs. automation readiness: what the data actually shows — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
RESEARCH
March 14, 2026
The Robot Age Editorial Team
Automation anxiety vs. automation readiness: what the data actually shows
Two narratives dominate the public conversation about robots and work. The first is anxiety: robots are coming for jobs, and there is nothing to be done. The second is denial: robots will create more jobs than they displace, so stop worrying. Both are wrong in the same way — they treat the outcome as inevitable rather than designed.
A survey of 1,400 workers across manufacturing, logistics, and healthcare found that anxiety about automation correlates more strongly with a lack of information than with actual job risk. Workers who reported high anxiety were not necessarily in roles most exposed to automation. They were in roles where no one had talked to them about what was changing.
Readiness, by contrast, correlated strongly with two factors: whether workers felt they understood what the robots in their environment were doing, and whether they had been involved in any part of the deployment process. Understanding and participation — not job security — were the primary predictors of positive adaptation.
This has direct implications for how organisations communicate about robot adoption. The instinct is often to minimise concern by emphasising job creation statistics. The data suggests a different approach works better: explain the robot, involve the people, and create structured ways for frontline workers to surface problems.
Automation anxiety is largely a design failure. It is what happens when deployment is done to people rather than with them. The good news is that it is fixable — and the fix does not require technical expertise. It requires communication, participation, and honest acknowledgement of what is changing and why.

title: The next earthquake rescue crew will have robots in the rubble. — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
text:
The next earthquake rescue crew will have robots in the rubble. — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
RESEARCH
August 14, 2026
The Robot Age Editorial Team
The next earthquake rescue crew will have robots in the rubble.
When an earthquake brings a building down, rescue becomes a race against voids, dust, unstable concrete, broken utilities, and time. The first 48 hours are the harshest part of that race. Survivors may be injured, dehydrated, trapped without light, or hidden under layers of rubble that crews cannot safely enter. The broader rescue window is often described as the first 48 to 72 hours, but every hour lost can shrink the chance of finding someone alive.
That is why the future of earthquake response cannot be limited to robot cameras or remote-controlled vehicles. The next leap is autonomous rescue robots that work beside human crews: mapping collapsed structures, detecting signs of life, prioritizing search zones, carrying sensors into unsafe voids, and helping incident commanders decide where to dig first.
Real disaster zones already changed the question
Robots have already been tested by real earthquakes. After the 2016 Amatrice earthquake in Italy, the EU-funded
TRADR project
deployed two unmanned ground vehicles and three drones at the request of the Italian fire brigade. Their work was practical rather than theatrical: collect images, build 3D context, inspect dangerous interiors, and help firefighters understand damaged structures without sending people into unsafe spaces.
TRADR's own
Amatrice field report
is useful because it shows what rescue robotics looks like outside a lab. The hard problems were not just locomotion. They were communications, human coordination, field setup, damage interpretation, and building trust with responders who had no time for fragile prototypes.
The lesson was clear: robots can earn a place in disaster response when they make crews faster, safer, and better informed. But that generation of systems was still mostly supervised. The robot extended the rescuer's eyes and reach. It did not yet behave like a field teammate.
AI turns search from passive viewing into active decisions
The next generation changes the role of the machine. A remote camera waits for a human to notice something. An AI-enabled rescue robot can decide where to look next.
Recent research on
active robotic search for victims
uses deep learning and probabilistic planning so a robot does not simply follow a fixed route through a disaster area. It estimates where victims are more likely to be, updates that estimate as it observes the scene, and chooses the next best viewpoint. Other work on search-and-rescue perception combines RGB, thermal, and multispectral imagery with deep learning to improve victim detection in cluttered, low-light, and partially occluded environments.
That matters under rubble because the bottleneck is not only access. It is attention. Rescue teams face too many voids, too many unstable paths, and too little certainty. A robot that can map, classify, and prioritize possible survivor locations can compress the search while human crews focus on extraction.
Quadrupeds are built for broken ground
Quadruped robots are especially relevant after earthquakes because rubble is hostile to wheels and tracks. Broken concrete, tilted slabs, stairs, gaps, loose debris, and exposed rebar create terrain where conventional ground robots can stall. Legged robots can step across discontinuous surfaces, recover balance, climb uneven paths, and carry payloads such as LiDAR, thermal cameras, microphones, gas sensors, radios, and small medical supplies.
That shift is already visible in the field. In Japan's 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake response, Japan's Ground Self-Defense Force deployed quadrupedal unmanned ground vehicles, according to a
Ghost Robotics case study
, for tasks including reconnaissance in unsafe areas, small-payload delivery, and communications support where infrastructure was damaged.
This is not the end state. It is the hinge. The first practical deployments prove that legged robots can enter the disaster workflow. The next step is giving them more autonomy so they can search with less constant teleoperation during the most chaotic hours of a response.
The autonomy proof point came from underground
The best preview of earthquake rescue autonomy may come from underground robotics. In the DARPA Subterranean Challenge, Team CERBERUS built a system of legged and flying robots designed to explore GPS-denied, communication-poor environments. The team combined LiDAR, cameras, inertial sensing, multi-robot mapping, and autonomy so one human supervisor could direct a robotic team through complex terrain.
The
CERBERUS system
and its
technical paper
matter because collapsed buildings create similar constraints: no GPS, poor communications, darkness, dust, blocked paths, unstable floors, and an urgent need to search more area than people can safely cover. The DARPA environment was a competition, not an earthquake. But the autonomy stack points directly at disaster response: robots that can explore, map, share information, and continue operating when communication with the human operator becomes unreliable.
Finding life through debris is the real prize
The most valuable rescue robot is not the one that looks impressive on rubble. It is the one that helps find a living person sooner.
That is why the history of NASA/JPL and DHS's FINDER technology matters. After the 2015 Nepal earthquake,
FINDER helped rescuers locate four men
trapped under rubble by detecting heartbeats through debris. FINDER was not an autonomous robot, but it proved a critical principle: life-saving information can be detected before rescuers physically reach a victim.
The next step is putting that kind of sensing on mobile, AI-guided platforms. A future earthquake response could combine quadrupeds crossing the rubble surface, drones mapping damaged structures from above, soft robots probing narrow cavities, and distributed sensors listening for breathing, tapping, heat, motion, CO2, or heartbeats. MIT Lincoln Laboratory's
SPROUT vine robot
points in that direction: a flexible robot designed to extend through tight spaces without forcing debris apart.
Robots beside rescuers, not instead of them
The strongest vision is not robots replacing rescue crews. It is robots working beside them.
Human crews bring structural judgment, medical skill, coordination, ethics, and the final responsibility of extracting a person safely. Robots bring endurance, repeatable scanning, hazardous access, fast mapping, and the ability to search places too dangerous for people or dogs. The value is the combination.
In the first 48 hours after an earthquake, that combination could matter more than almost any other robotic use case. A quadruped robot can enter an unstable zone before a team commits people. A drone can build a live exterior map. A soft robot can push a sensor deeper into a void. An AI system can fuse the signals into a ranked search map. A human commander can then decide where to send the next crew, which slab to stabilize, and which void deserves immediate excavation.
The technology is not fully solved. Batteries, dust, water, debris, radio failure, sensor reliability, certification, responder training, and public trust remain serious barriers. A disaster zone is not a demo floor. A rescue robot has to work when the ground is broken, the network is gone, and lives depend on boring reliability.
But the direction is now visible. Earthquake rescue robots are moving beyond eyes on wheels. They are becoming autonomous teammates for the people who run toward collapsed buildings when everyone else is running away.

It estimates where victims are more likely to be, updates that estimate as it observes the scene, and chooses the next best viewpoint. Other work on search-and-rescue perception combines RGB, thermal, and multispectral imagery with deep learning to improve victim detection in cluttered, low-light, and partially occluded environments.
That matters under rubble because the bottleneck is not only access. It is attention. Rescue teams face too many voids, too many unstable paths, and too little certainty. A robot that can map, classify, and prioritize possible survivor locations can compress the search while human crews focus on extraction.
Quadrupeds are built for broken ground
Quadruped robots are especially relevant after earthquakes because rubble is hostile to wheels and tracks. Broken concrete, tilted slabs, stairs, gaps, loose debris, and exposed rebar create terrain where conventional ground robots can stall. Legged robots can step across discontinuous surfaces, recover balance, climb uneven paths, and carry payloads such as LiDAR, thermal cameras, microphones, gas sensors, radios, and small medical supplies.
That shift is already visible in the field. In Japan's 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake response, Japan's Ground Self-Defense Force deployed quadrupedal unmanned ground vehicles, according to a
Ghost Robotics case study
, for tasks including reconnaissance in unsafe areas, small-payload delivery, and communications support where infrastructure was damaged.
This is not the end state. It is the hinge. The first practical deployments prove that legged robots can enter the disaster workflow. The next step is giving them more autonomy so they can search with less constant teleoperation during the most chaotic hours of a response.
The autonomy proof point came from underground
The best preview of earthquake rescue autonomy may come from underground robotics. In the DARPA Subterranean Challenge, Team CERBERUS built a system of legged and flying robots designed to explore GPS-denied, communication-poor environments. The team combined LiDAR, cameras, inertial sensing, multi-robot mapping, and autonomy so one human supervisor could direct a robotic team through complex terrain.
The
CERBERUS system
and its
technical paper
matter because collapsed buildings create similar constraints: no GPS, poor communications, darkness, dust, blocked paths, unstable floors, and an urgent need to search more area than people can safely cover. The DARPA environment was a competition, not an earthquake. But the autonomy stack points directly at disaster response: robots that can explore, map, share information, and continue operating when communication with the human operator becomes unreliable.
Finding life through debris is the real prize
The most valuable rescue robot is not the one that looks impressive on rubble. It is the one that helps find a living person sooner.
That is why the history of NASA/JPL and DHS's FINDER technology matters. After the 2015 Nepal earthquake,
FINDER helped rescuers locate four men
trapped under rubble by detecting heartbeats through debris. FINDER was not an autonomous robot, but it proved a critical principle: life-saving information can be detected before rescuers physically reach a victim.
The next step is putting that kind of sensing on mobile, AI-guided platforms. A future earthquake response could combine quadrupeds crossing the rubble surface, drones mapping damaged structures from above, soft robots probing narrow cavities, and distributed sensors listening for breathing, tapping, heat, motion, CO2, or heartbeats. MIT Lincoln Laboratory's
SPROUT vine robot
points in that direction: a flexible robot designed to extend through tight spaces without forcing debris apart.
Robots beside rescuers, not instead of them
The strongest vision is not robots replacing rescue crews. It is robots working beside them.
Human crews bring structural judgment, medical skill, coordination, ethics, and the final responsibility of extracting a person safely. Robots bring endurance, repeatable scanning, hazardous access, fast mapping, and the ability to search places too dangerous for people or dogs. The value is the combination.
In the first 48 hours after an earthquake, that combination could matter more than almost any other robotic use case. A quadruped robot can enter an unstable zone before a team commits people. A drone can build a live exterior map. A soft robot can push a sensor deeper into a void. An AI system can fuse the signals into a ranked search map. A human commander can then decide where to send the next crew, which slab to stabilize, and which void deserves immediate excavation.
The technology is not fully solved. Batteries, dust, water, debris, radio failure, sensor reliability, certification, responder training, and public trust remain serious barriers. A disaster zone is not a demo floor. A rescue robot has to work when the ground is broken, the network is gone, and lives depend on boring reliability.
But the direction is now visible. Earthquake rescue robots are moving beyond eyes on wheels. They are becoming autonomous teammates for the people who run toward collapsed buildings when everyone else is running away.

title: Robotics is national policy now. — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
text:
Robotics is national policy now. — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
NEWS
August 10, 2026
The Robot Age Editorial Team
Robotics is national policy now.
China's humanoid robot target puts the pressure where robotics gets real: deployment.
Caixin reported
that China wants more than 10,000 humanoid robots in commercial use by the end of 2026, across more than 100 application scenarios.
Ten thousand robots will not remake Chinese industry this year. The number matters because it creates a field test large enough to expose the practical work: maintenance, staff training, failure recovery, safety procedures, procurement, uptime, replacement parts, and the question every operations lead eventually asks — does the robot earn its space?
China has chosen deployment as the forcing function. Local governments can host pilots. State-owned enterprises can become early buyers. Manufacturers, logistics operators, hospitals, and service venues can be directed into structured tests. Even weak deployments produce useful information when the machines leave the lab and meet shift work, crowded aisles, tired staff, and real failure modes.
The United States has no matching national deployment target. It has strong companies, labs, chips, simulation tools, and robotics software, but its policy response is still forming through private investment, agency rules, and legislation. The proposed
National Commission on Robotics Act
would study U.S. competitiveness and recommend a strategy. That is useful. It is not a deployment plan.
This is the gap. China is asking whether humanoids can be put to work at scale. The U.S. is asking how to organize its robotics response. Both questions matter, but they produce different learning loops. A commission can clarify priorities. A field deployment tells product teams which grippers break, which tasks need redesign, which workers need orientation, and which buyers reorder.
The robot ban cuts both ways
The U.S. ban on foreign-made advanced robots changes the incentive map. The
Associated Press reported
that new restrictions on foreign-made humanoids and related systems are aimed largely at China. The security concern is clear: a connected robot is a mobile sensor platform with cameras, microphones, mapping, network access, remote updates, and physical agency.
Blocking Chinese robots may protect sensitive American environments. It may also push Chinese firms deeper into their home market. If U.S. buyers become harder to reach, Chinese companies can design around Chinese factories, Chinese logistics networks, Chinese hospitals, Chinese public procurement, and Chinese service teams. That narrows the brief and brings the manufacturer closer to the deployment site.
That domestic loop could matter more than near-term exports. Robots improve when the people who build them can watch how they fail, repair them quickly, change the workflow, and push the next version into the same kind of site. A ban reduces one market. It can also concentrate the learning.
The U.S. needs the defensive policy and the build plan. Restrictions can keep untrusted robots out of sensitive spaces. They cannot create domestic production capacity, field technicians, safety evidence, buyer confidence, or deployment literacy by themselves.
China's 10,000-robot target may miss, overcount, or produce uneven results. It still gives the sector what demos cannot: enough real-world contact to find out which robots belong in the room.

title: Digit 5 shows why humanoid design is really trust design — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
text:
Digit 5 shows why humanoid design is really trust design — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
OPINION
September 16, 2026
The Robot Age Editorial Team
Digit 5 shows why humanoid design is really trust design
Listen to this article
Your browser does not support audio playback.
AI-generated narration
Agility Robotics has become one of the few humanoid companies that can say more than "watch the demo." Digit has worked inside real warehouses, moved real totes, and given the company something most humanoid startups still lack: operating evidence. With
Digit 5
, Agility is now making a more subtle argument. The robot is not only getting more capable. It is getting more readable.
That matters because people do not experience robots as spec sheets. They read posture, motion, body proportions, directionality, and apparent attention before they understand payload, fleet software, or unit economics. In human-robot environments, form is never just styling. Form tells nearby people what the machine is, what it is about to do, and whether it belongs beside them.
Digit 5 is a useful case study in RXD: Robot Experience Design. The question is not simply whether the robot can walk, carry, and coordinate across a facility. The question is whether its body helps people understand it accurately.
The head is the attention signal
The head is the most important nonfunctional part of a humanoid robot. It may contain sensors, cameras, compute, or perception hardware, but its effect on humans is older than any of those systems. People look for a head because the head tells them where attention is directed.
Digit's head design has always been restrained. It does not try to be a face. That restraint is the right instinct. A face would suggest emotional intelligence, social reciprocity, and conversational competence that a warehouse humanoid does not need to promise. A blank sensor pod, by contrast, can still give people a place to read orientation: this is where the robot is pointed, this is where it may be perceiving from, this is the part of the body that frames its awareness.
Digit 5 makes that design decision more important, not less. Agility is positioning the robot around "cooperatively safe work" near people. That means the robot's body must make its behavior legible before a worker has to reason about it. Is the robot paused? Is it yielding? Is it about to step into the aisle? Has it noticed the person beside it? A head that functions as an attention marker can reduce ambiguity even without expression.
The RXD risk is overpromise. When a machine has a head, humans begin to assign intention to it. They may assume it sees more than it sees, understands more than it understands, or is making a judgment rather than executing a constrained behavior. Good humanoid head design should communicate orientation and state without pretending to be a person.
The legs are the trust problem
Digit's legs are Agility's real brand. Most warehouse robots roll. Digit walks. That choice instantly changes how people understand the robot. Legs imply adaptability. Legs imply access to human-designed environments. Legs imply that the machine can move through a facility without the facility being rebuilt around it.
They also raise the standard for trust.
Humans are expert readers of bipedal motion. A wheeled autonomous mobile robot can move awkwardly and still feel like equipment. A humanoid that hesitates, wobbles, recovers slowly, or places a foot strangely can feel vulnerable or unsafe even if it is technically functioning. We do not only see motion; we read balance, effort, confidence, and risk.
That makes Digit 5's lower body central to the experience story. Its legs are not just mobility hardware. They are a trust interface. Smooth gait says competence. Stable posture says safety. Controlled foot placement says the robot belongs around people and assets. The move away from the older backward-bending leg silhouette toward a more human-readable stance changes the signal: Digit 5 looks less like a novel mechanism and more like an industrial body designed to lift, squat, pause, and share space.
That boundary matters. The wrong humanoid design can fall into expectation mismatch: it looks like it should move with human grace, reason with human judgment, and recover with human improvisation. Digit's best design move is that it does not chase realism. It chases workplace readability.
Digit 5, Agility's fifth-generation humanoid platform. Image: Agility Robotics
Technical profile
Digit 5
Agility Robotics · Salem, Oregon
The fifth-generation Digit humanoid is positioned for cooperatively safe industrial work near people, extending the platform from fixed pilots toward full facility workflows.
Form factor
Bipedal industrial humanoid
Primary role
Material handling in warehouses, factories, and logistics sites
Design signal
Non-face head for attention, sensing, and orientation legibility
Mobility signal
Redesigned bipedal legs for lifting, squatting, and human-scale work zones
Fleet system
Agility Arc for deployment, monitoring, and workflow management
Safety frame
Cooperatively safe work near people and assets
Operating history
Built on 65,000+ hours of Digit field operation
Orders
$300M+ in multi-year Digit 5 orders, subject to milestones
Manufacturing
RoboFab facility designed for up to 10,000 robots per year at full capacity
Economic test
Must prove uptime, service cost, throughput, and repeatable ROI
Human form creates human expectations
The reason humanoid design is powerful is the same reason it is dangerous. The human brain does not wait for a technical explanation. If something has a head, torso, arms, and legs, people begin assigning intention to it. They ask, often unconsciously: Is it looking at me? Is it coming toward me? Is it struggling? Is it safe? Does it understand the space we are sharing?
This is where robot literacy matters. A humanoid is not a human worker in a metal body. It is a machine using human form as an interface to a human environment. That interface can be useful when it helps people predict the robot's behavior. It becomes misleading when it implies competence the system does not yet have.
Agility's marketing works because Digit has a clear job. It is not being sold as a household companion or a general social agent. It is being sold into repetitive industrial work: moving totes, carrying containers, navigating workflows built around human-height infrastructure. The form matches the pitch. The head does not need a smile. The legs do not need ballet. The robot needs to communicate: I can move, pause, yield, lift, repeat, and be supervised.
That is why Digit 5's form improvements matter more than a feature checklist. The head and legs are the parts workers will read first. They define whether the robot feels purposeful or uncanny, controlled or fragile, useful or theatrical.
The marketing is strong because the form is legible
Agility is very good at making Digit feel real. The company's message is simple: this is a humanoid already shaped by production floors, now upgraded for safer and broader deployment. That is cleaner than the usual humanoid pitch, where a robot performs one striking task and the audience is asked to imagine the rest of the business.
But strong marketing creates its own pressure.
The Robot Report
notes that Agility's filings describe a large leap from today's revenue to future deployment targets.
Business Insider
reported an illustrative ownership model near $200,000 upfront, plus deployment and ongoing software and maintenance costs. That does not make the robot unserious. It makes the design stakes higher.
At that price, a humanoid cannot merely look convincing. It has to be understood quickly, trusted appropriately, maintained efficiently, and productive enough to justify its presence. The body has to help the business case.
The robot age will be designed before it is accepted
Digit 5 shows that humanoid robotics is entering a design phase. The early question was whether a robot like Digit could work at all. Agility has evidence that it can. The next question is whether the form can scale socially and economically inside real facilities.
That is where RXD becomes practical. Readability asks whether workers can interpret the robot at a glance. Expectation asks whether the humanlike form promises more intelligence or dexterity than the system can deliver. Deployment asks whether the design lowers friction in the actual workplace: fewer misunderstandings, fewer training burdens, fewer safety concerns, better acceptance.
Digit 5's most important upgrade may not be what it can lift. It may be what it communicates. In the robot age, form is not decoration. Form is how humans decide whether a machine belongs beside them.

title: Home humanoid safety has a relationship problem. — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
text:
Home humanoid safety has a relationship problem. — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
NEWS
July 1, 2026
The Robot Age Editorial Team
Home humanoid safety has a relationship problem.
Domestic humanoid safety is no longer a question of whether the robot can avoid hitting someone. It is becoming a question of whether the whole relationship stays safe when the robot, the human, and the room keep changing.
IEEE Spectrum reported
that ISO is updating the 12-year-old safety requirements behind ISO 13482, the standard historically aimed at personal care robots. The update matters because home robots are moving from research platforms and carefully staged demos toward products meant for real families, older adults, caregivers, visitors, and children.

Loughborough University release

now describes safety requirements for service robots used in personal and professional or commercial settings, excluding industrial and medical robots. notes a specific problem with default emergency-stop assumptions: cutting power to a legged robot can create a new hazard if the robot falls.

The U.S. workplace rulebook is not ready to absorb domestic humanoids either.
OSHA says
there are currently no specific OSHA standards for the robotics industry. Its robotics page points instead to related rules for walking-working surfaces, occupational noise, personal protective equipment, lockout/tagout, machine guarding, electrical safety, and state-plan standards.
Those rules matter for warehouses, hospitals, labs, and care facilities. They also show how patchwork the near future will be. A humanoid in a logistics facility may be evaluated through industrial robot, mobile robot, machine guarding, and lockout/tagout lenses. A similar body in a home may fall under consumer product safety, privacy law, disability services, product liability, insurance requirements, and voluntary certification.
For product teams, that means "safe enough" will not be a single pass-fail question. It will require evidence across operating domains: who the robot is safe around, which rooms it can enter, which users it can assist, what it does when confused, how teleoperation is disclosed, how it logs incidents, and when it must stop asking the user to adapt.
The practical risks are ordinary
The most important domestic risks will look mundane. A robot that backs up while carrying laundry may trip a child sitting on the floor. A caregiver may assume the robot has seen a walker when it has not. A user with dementia may treat a prompt as instruction rather than suggestion. A pet may move under the robot during a turn. A kitchen spill may turn a normal step into a fall event.
Loose clothing, blankets, charging cords, toys, rugs, thresholds, and open cabinet doors are not edge cases. They are the baseline condition of domestic robotics. A standard that tests a humanoid in a clean room with healthy adults is not testing the thing buyers are being sold.
The emotional layer adds another failure mode. If a robot speaks with confidence, follows a person, reminds them to take medication, or offers companionship, users may treat its behavior as more capable than it is. UX design becomes safety design. The robot has to communicate uncertainty, limitations, handoff points, and failure states without shifting hidden operational burden onto the person least able to carry it.
The missing test is safe behavior over time
The standards gap is not that no one knows robots can injure people. The gap is that current standards struggle to define safe relational behavior over time. A domestic humanoid may be safe in a lab trial, then become risky after a furniture change, a software update, a new caregiver, a child's visit, or a shift in the user's health.
That pushes safety toward ongoing assurance. Product teams will need scenario libraries, incident reporting, household onboarding, safe teleoperation indicators, privacy controls, maintenance rules, and user feedback loops. Regulators and insurers will need ways to ask whether the robot remained safe after deployment, not just whether it passed a pre-market checklist.
The next home-robot standard should make one assumption explicit: the human is part of the system. Once that is admitted, the design work changes. Safety is no longer only a property of the machine. It is a property of the machine, the person, the room, and the interaction between them.

title: The Delivery Robot Is Splitting in Two — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
text:
The Delivery Robot Is Splitting in Two — The Robot Age — The Robot Age
OPINION
September 30, 2026
The Robot Age Editorial Team
The Delivery Robot Is Splitting in Two
Listen to this article
Your browser does not support audio playback.
AI-generated narration
Autonomous delivery no longer has one shape. It has a sky version and a sidewalk version.
Lowe's is now testing drone delivery with DoorDash and Wing from a store in Matthews, North Carolina, near Charlotte. Customers can order eligible home-improvement items through the DoorDash app and have small orders delivered by Wing drones in as fast as 20 minutes. The payload is modest, about 2.5 pounds per flight, but that is exactly the point: a tube of caulk, batteries, painter's tape, a screwdriver, or another small project item does not need a car.
At the same time, DoorDash is building the other lane. Its partnership with Coco Robotics is live in Los Angeles and Chicago, after a Wolt pilot in Helsinki, with sidewalk robots available from nearly 600 participating merchants. Coco says it has completed more than 100,000 deliveries for DoorDash customers and operates more than 1,000 delivery robots. DoorDash has also unveiled Dot, its own in-house robot designed to travel through bike lanes, roads, sidewalks, and driveways at up to 20 mph in early access deployments around Tempe and Mesa, Arizona.
Robot.com, formerly Kiwibot, is proving a related ground model in Canada. In Markham, Ontario, Real Life Robotics and Skip are running a three-month robot delivery pilot using supervised robots developed with Robot.com, operating within a two-kilometer radius of participating restaurants. The robots use secure compartments, QR-code handoff, teleoperation support, and all-weather operation.
This is not one delivery revolution. It is two public-space claims arriving at once: drones in the air, robots on the ground.
The sky route solves distance, then inherits aviation
Drone delivery is seductive because it skips the messy ground layer. A drone does not get stuck behind a double-parked truck. It does not wait at a crosswalk. It does not weave around strollers, scooters, patio seating, tree pits, snow banks, or a person walking a dog.
That makes the Lowe's, DoorDash, and Wing pilot easy to understand. For small, urgent items, the sky is a shortcut. A drone can turn a quick errand into a short flight.
But the sky is not empty. Drone delivery inherits the rules and anxieties of aviation. The regulatory questions are about airspace, certification, operator responsibility, beyond-visual-line-of-sight operation, aircraft reliability, weather, drop zones, noise, and what it means for machines with cameras and propellers to pass repeatedly over homes.
The cultural question is even more basic: people may accept a truck on the street because streets are already delivery infrastructure. They may not feel the same way about aircraft above a backyard.
This is the drone paradox. The machine avoids the sidewalk, but becomes more intimate in another way. It enters the acoustic and visual space above private life. A sidewalk robot is visible and negotiable. A drone is heard first, then seen overhead.
That matters. Communities will not judge drone delivery only by crash rates. They will judge it by sound, privacy, nuisance, weather failures, emergency response, and whether the convenience feels evenly shared or mostly imposed on neighborhoods for someone else's instant gratification.
The land route solves handoff, then inherits the sidewalk
Sidewalk robots solve a different problem. They are not trying to fly over the last mile. They are trying to make the last mile smaller, cheaper, slower, and more local.
Coco's DoorDash rollout is the cleanest example. Small food orders do not need a two-ton car, as DoorDash Labs has put it. A sidewalk robot can wait outside a restaurant, roll a short urban route, and hand off to a customer without taking a parking space or burning a gallon of gas.
Dot pushes the same logic harder. DoorDash describes it as a compact autonomous vehicle that can move through bike lanes, roads, sidewalks, and driveways, one-tenth the size of a car, fast enough for local trips but small enough for neighborhood handoffs. That hybrid form is important. It is not only a sidewalk robot. It is a machine asking for access to multiple human lanes at once.
Robot.com's Markham deployment shows the more civic version of the same idea. Four supervised robots, a defined delivery radius, secure compartments, municipal approval, teleoperation, and a limited pilot period. That is the shape early robot delivery should have: bounded, observable, and tied to local rules.
The ground robot has a different regulatory burden than the drone. It needs rules for sidewalk right-of-way, speed, weight, stopping behavior, accessibility, insurance, remote supervision, retrieval, data collection, and how it behaves at intersections. It also needs a social contract. Who yields when a robot meets a wheelchair user on a narrow sidewalk? What happens when kids crowd around it? Who is responsible if it blocks a curb cut? Can it wait outside a building without becoming street clutter?
The robot may be small, but the public-space question is large.
China treated delivery robots as infrastructure, not gadgets
The most useful comparison is not another American pilot. It is China.
JD.com, Meituan, Alibaba, and Neolix began treating autonomous delivery as part of urban logistics years ago. In Beijing's Yizhuang pilot zone, authorities allowed JD.com, Meituan, and Neolix to test zero-occupant delivery vehicles on designated public roads. Those vehicles were categorized as "non-motor vehicles," putting them closer to bicycles and e-scooters than cars, and the rules required safety drivers both on site and remotely.
That sounds bureaucratic. It is actually the important part.
China did not simply ask whether the robot worked. Cities began asking what lane it belongs in, how it should be supervised, where it can stop, what infrastructure helps it move safely, and how public agencies learn from deployment data. The Center for Data Innovation argues that Beijing has gone further than most U.S. jurisdictions by creating a 225-square-kilometer policy pilot zone, building smart sidewalks with roadside sensors, subsidizing high-liability insurance for operators, and tying robot policy to cybersecurity, jobs, and urban planning.
That does not mean the Chinese model transfers cleanly to the United States. It does not. American cities have different legal systems, property expectations, disability-rights rules, street politics, and tolerance for surveillance infrastructure. But China offers a lesson: sidewalk robots scale when cities treat them as infrastructure participants, not toys.
Japan offers the same lesson in a quieter way. Its delivery-robot rules have emphasized low speeds and remote monitoring. The point is not speed. The point is public compatibility.
Protection goes both ways
Most robot regulation focuses on protecting people from machines. Delivery robots also force the inverse question: how do cities protect machines from people without giving machines too much priority?
This sounds strange until the robots arrive. People kick them. Block them. Ride them. Film them. Try to open them. Move traffic cones in front of them. Treat them like a prank object, a nuisance, or a public toy.
That behavior is not only a business problem. It is a civic design problem. If a robot is allowed into shared space, the operator needs a way to retrieve it, identify it, insure it, receive complaints, and prove what happened. The public needs rules against tampering and theft. But those rules should not turn every sidewalk encounter into a police issue, and they should not let companies privatize pedestrian space.
The right balance is simple to state and hard to write into law: protect people first, protect access second, protect the robot third.
That means low speeds near pedestrians, clear yielding behavior, audible or visible signals that do not become noise pollution, accessible reporting, remote-assist requirements, local operating permits, insurance, crash and blockage reporting, and penalties for deliberate vandalism or theft. It also means caps, routes, or geofences in crowded districts where the sidewalk is already overloaded.
The cultural shift is bigger than the delivery
Delivery robots will change more than logistics.
Drones make delivery feel like weather. They appear above a neighborhood, make a sound, drop something, and leave. They may become normal quickly, or they may become one more ambient intrusion in communities already tired of cameras, alerts, and machines that optimize someone else's convenience.
Sidewalk robots are different. They become street characters. People name them. Kids point at them. Restaurants learn their rhythms. Some neighbors will find them charming. Others will see them as clutter, labor displacement, surveillance, or another example of public infrastructure being used for private commerce.
The labor question matters. DoorDash says Dashers will remain essential and that autonomous systems can handle lower-value local trips while humans focus on higher-value deliveries that require judgment and care. That may be true at first. But the long-term social question is whether robot delivery creates better work around supervision, maintenance, loading, cleaning, and fleet operations, or simply removes the lowest-margin trips from people who already live on thin margins.
The equity question matters too. Which neighborhoods get the fast drone lane? Which neighborhoods get sidewalk robots? Which communities become test beds, and which get to say no? Are these systems built for dense, wealthy, app-native districts first, or for people who actually need better delivery access because of age, disability, poor transit, or distance from retail?
The technology is not neutral once it enters a sidewalk or a sky lane. It changes who waits, who yields, who is watched, who is served, and who is asked to tolerate the experiment.
The Robot Age view
The future of autonomous delivery will not be decided by whether drones are cooler than sidewalk robots. The real contest is regulatory fit.
Drones need airspace permission, noise acceptance, safe drop zones, and public trust over private property. Ground robots need sidewalk permission, disability-safe behavior, low-speed etiquette, theft protection, insurance, and a way to avoid becoming moving clutter.
One claims the sky. One claims the curb. Both claim public space.
That is the robot-literacy question for communities: not "Can the robot deliver?" but "Which lane is it asking for, who already depends on that lane, and what rules make the exchange fair?"
The best delivery robot will not be the one that moves fastest. It will be the one that communities can understand, regulate, live with, and trust after the novelty wears off.

DoorDash says Dashers will remain essential and that autonomous systems can handle lower-value local trips while humans focus on higher-value deliveries that require judgment and care. That may be true at first. But the long-term social question is whether robot delivery creates better work around supervision, maintenance, loading, cleaning, and fleet operations, or simply removes the lowest-margin trips from people who already live on thin margins.
The equity question matters too. Which neighborhoods get the fast drone lane? Which neighborhoods get sidewalk robots? Which communities become test beds, and which get to say no? Are these systems built for dense, wealthy, app-native districts first, or for people who actually need better delivery access because of age, disability, poor transit, or distance from retail?
The technology is not neutral once it enters a sidewalk or a sky lane. It changes who waits, who yields, who is watched, who is served, and who is asked to tolerate the experiment.
The Robot Age view
The future of autonomous delivery will not be decided by whether drones are cooler than sidewalk robots. The real contest is regulatory fit.
Drones need airspace permission, noise acceptance, safe drop zones, and public trust over private property. Ground robots need sidewalk permission, disability-safe behavior, low-speed etiquette, theft protection, insurance, and a way to avoid becoming moving clutter.
One claims the sky. One claims the curb. Both claim public space.
That is the robot-literacy question for communities: not "Can the robot deliver?" but "Which lane is it asking for, who already depends on that lane, and what rules make the exchange fair?"
The best delivery robot will not be the one that moves fastest. It will be the one that communities can understand, regulate, live with, and trust after the novelty wears off.
